Job Title: AI Infrastructure SpecialistLocation: United States (Remote)Work Mode: 100% RemoteExperience: 2–6 YearsSalary Range: $95,000 – $155,000 per year (USD)Employment Type: Full-TimeJob Category: Artificial Intelligence / Cloud Infrastructure / DevOps.

Industry observers note that we are seeking a skilled and experienced AI Infrastructure Specialist to join our growing technology team in the United States. The ideal candidate will be responsible for designing, building, deploying, and maintaining scalable infrastructure to support AI and machine learning workloads.

In a recent development, the candidate should have strong knowledge of cloud infrastructure, GPU computing, containerization, Kubernetes, MLOps, and AI model deployment. This role involves optimizing infrastructure performance, ensuring scalability, and supporting reliable AI-powered applications.

This position offers a fully remote work opportunity for qualified candidates across the United States.

Design, deploy, and maintain scalable infrastructure for AI and machine learning applications.

Manage cloud-based AI infrastructure across AWS, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud.

Configure and optimize GPU-based computing environments for AI workloads.

Implement and maintain Kubernetes clusters and Docker containers.

Support AI model training, deployment, and inference environments.

Build and maintain MLOps pipelines for continuous integration and deployment.

Monitor infrastructure performance, availability, scalability, and resource utilization.

Optimize GPU, CPU, memory, and storage resources for AI workloads.

Implement infrastructure automation using Terraform, Ansible, or similar tools.

Collaborate with AI engineers, ML engineers, and DevOps teams.

Implement infrastructure security, access controls, and monitoring solutions.

Troubleshoot infrastructure challenges and ensure system reliability.

Maintain technical documentation and infrastructure best practices.

2–6 years of experience in AI Infrastructure, Cloud Infrastructure, DevOps, or a related field.

Strong knowledge of AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud platforms.

Hands-on experience with Docker and Kubernetes.

Understanding of GPU computing and AI workload optimization.

Experience with Linux administration and system troubleshooting.

Knowledge of Python, Bash, or Shell scripting.

Familiarity with machine learning model deployment and inference workflows.

Experience with CI/CD pipelines and infrastructure automation.

Knowledge of Terraform, Ansible, or similar infrastructure tools.

Understanding of networking, storage, and cloud security fundamentals.

Experience with monitoring tools such as Prometheus, Grafana, or Datadog.

Strong analytical, troubleshooting, and problem-solving skills.

Bachelor's or Master's degree in Computer Science, Information Technology, Engineering, or a related field.

Experience with NVIDIA GPUs, CUDA, and GPU resource management.

Familiarity with MLflow, Kubeflow, Ray, or similar MLOps frameworks.

Knowledge of LLM deployment and inference optimization.

Experience with distributed computing and high-performance computing (HPC).

Familiarity with serverless AI infrastructure and microservices architecture.

Understanding of model serving frameworks such as NVIDIA Triton, vLLM, or TorchServe.

Experience managing large-scale AI infrastructure environments.

Annual Salary: $95,000 – $155,000 USD.

Competitive compensation based on experience and technical expertise.

Health, dental, and vision insurance.

Retirement savings benefits, where applicable.

Professional development and technical certification support.

Career advancement opportunities.

Candidates from eligible locations across the United States are encouraged to apply.

Must be legally authorized to work in the United States.

Ability to collaborate with distributed engineering teams across different US time zones.

Interested candidates can submit their updated resume along with contact details, relevant AI Infrastructure experience, and certifications or project portfolios.

Equal Opportunity Employer: We welcome qualified candidates from diverse professional backgrounds and encourage applications from eligible candidates across the United States.

Elon Musk’s Grokipedia is littered with mistakes. But Wikipedia could still learn some things from it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

Nearly there — check your email.

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Grokipedia shows that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet.

Recent findings suggest that when I saw Grokipedia’s articles about me, the memories came rushing back: my 19 years in minor league baseball, including that impressive season with the Montgomery Rebels when I hit 20 home runs. I was lean back then — 6 feet tall and 168 pounds — and earned a career batting average just under .300. I became a minor league coach and managed the Chicago White Sox for a short stint in 1970, which Grokipedia said “highlighted [my] readiness for higher-level responsibilities.”.

I then attended Arizona State University, switched to a career in journalism, created the fact-checking site PolitiFact, won a Pulitzer Prize, and now teach journalism at Duke University.

Ah, the memories!…except that I never played minor league baseball, never managed the White Sox, and can only dream about being 6 feet tall. (I’m 5’8″.) Grokipedia, the AI-written encyclopedia of Elon Musk, has confused me with Marion Danne “Bill” Adair, who died in 2002.

Sources indicate that that article and another one about “Bill Adair (journalist)” — which really is me — illustrate the many flaws of Grokipedia, which rolled out a year ago. The articles are littered with mistakes and superfluous details. They are terribly written and ridiculously long. If Grok, the AI engine that wrote this turgid prose, were a student in one of my writing courses, I would give it a D. (Editor’s note: After this article was published, someone updated the inaccurate Grok pages. The original versions are linked here.).

Still, the articles provide valuable lessons for Wikipedia editors who are debating how and when to use AI. Grokipedia adds fresh content and context that Wikipedia often lacks. It shows that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet and summarizing them in sweeping prose. It can also provide balance to articles that need it.

Grok can’t write worth a lick, but it highlights how Wikipedia can take advantage of AI at a time when overworked editors are trying to keep the encyclopedia alive.

Industry observers note that musk rolled out Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he said was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet. With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a new version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.” When Grokipedia launched, Musk said he had significant aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video. Maybe someday. For now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes, peddle conspiracy theories, rely on low-credibility sources, and sometimes skew to the right. And although Grokipedia highlights edit requests from readers and whether they are approved, the site is not as transparent as Wikipedia, which reveals details about its editors and every change they make. Last spring, Grokipedia mysteriously stopped updating, according to a report by researchers Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson. It resumed in late September, still a hot mess, but with a more colorful homepage that always seems to feature its article about Musk. Grokipedia has two articles about me: the conflated baseball player one and “Bill Adair (journalist),” the real one, which is incredibly boring, even to me. Both borrow heavily from Wikipedia’s articles about us and enrich them with details found on assorted websites. Wikipedia’s article about me is nicely concise — just 700 words. It is written in the encyclopedia’s signature dry style and doesn’t contain any errors. The article recounts my career, some of the major news events I’ve covered, the two books I’ve written, and the awards I’ve won. But it highlights trivial events from my career, fails to emphasize larger ones, and lacks any criticism of my work. (I have not tried to improve the article because Wikipedia’s conflict of interest policy prohibits people from editing their own bios.) By contrast, Grokipedia’s “Bill Adair (journalist)” is painfully long — 5,600 words. Its greatest value would be to help someone suffering from a sleep disorder. Like a college student trying to meet a word count, Grok stuffed the article with needless details and redundant descriptions. The article tells you about my work with PolitiFact and then tells you again and again. It explains the site’s rating scale eight times and mentions my academic title four times. Despite labels that say “fact-checked by Grok,” both articles had lots of errors. I spotted 32 in the journalist one and so many in the baseball mashup that I couldn’t count them all. Mistakes are not surprising in AI writing, but I discovered interesting patterns that reveal the weaknesses of large language models. In the article about the real me, only seven of the errors were hallucinations in which Grok seemed to create a detail out of thin air. No, I did not win an award from Manhattan College, and no, PolitiFact did not begin by fact-checking the Tampa mayor’s race. Five other errors highlighted Grok was a lazy researcher that did not look broadly enough to check a claim. Grok said I am the director of Duke’s journalism program, but I left that job five years ago. The sources cited in the article don’t explain Grok’s mistake, so it seems likely it remembered an old announcement and failed to see a newer one that named my successor. The most prevalent errors were in a broad category I’d all cluelessness. These mistakes showed Grok didn’t fully understand what it read, like someone who skimmed an article too quickly. My favorite in this category was when I got credit for a big scoop in 2000 that George W. Bush had a DUI conviction, which the Grokipedia article said had an impact on “late-election discourse.” I wish! Yes, I was among the many journalists who covered that story, but I had no scoop. Together, the errors reveal that Grok is a knucklehead. It doesn’t know what’s important and what’s not. It is simply mashing together details from many web articles about me. Grok only knows what it found on the internet and it lacks experience and perspective to sort out what’s important. The writing is dreadful. The articles read as if Grok was trained on too many online resumes and corporate memos. Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.” Take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter. Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia. The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches. Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”) Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia. Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version. Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty. Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR. My big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles. After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities. Bill Adair, the Knight Professor of the Practice of Journalism and Public Policy at Duke University, is writing a book about how Wikipedia editors are adapting to the age of AI.

Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches.

Industry observers note that wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”).

Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia.

Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version.

In a recent development, grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty.

According to recent reports, musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR.

Industry observers note that my significant takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles.

After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities.

Bill Adair, the Knight Professor of the Practice of Journalism and Public Policy at Duke University, is writing a book about how Wikipedia editors are adapting to the age of AI.

Meta & OpenAI Agents Made Nearly 90% Of Agent Requests In Bot Data via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that AI agents from Meta and OpenAI made nearly 90% of the agent requests reaching sites and apps protected by HUMAN Security in October, according to the organization’s monthly State of Agentic Traffic report.
  • Recent findings suggest that in October, total agent requests were approximately 8 times greater than in August and roughly 2.6 times greater than September’s.
  • The majority of these requests accessed product and search content.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that AI agents from Meta and OpenAI made nearly 90% of the agent requests reaching sites and apps protected by HUMAN Security in October, according to the organization’s monthly State of Agentic Traffic report. Meta’s Muse accounted for 59% on its own.

Recent findings suggest that in October, total agent requests were approximately 8 times greater than in August and roughly 2.6 times greater than September’s. This report includes agent requests on HUMAN-protected sites and apps but does not include all internet traffic; each request represents an action by the agent, such as a page load or a search.

The majority of these requests accessed product and search content. There was a very small portion that reached the checkout area.

In a recent development, muse’s share of agent requests rose 19 percentage points from September, and the number of requests it sent nearly quadrupled. The report claims Muse now sends 3.7 times as many requests as ChatGPT Agent, the next-largest agent. Meta introduced Muse on Sept. 8.

According to recent reports, openAI accounted for about 30% of total requests with three of the top 10 agents. ChatGPT Agent had 28.5% of requests in September, but despite sending 44% more requests, its share dropped to 15.9% as Muse grew faster, according to the report. The Codex Browser application increased from 7.7% to 8.8% and the Codex Chrome extension went up from 3.3% to 5.2%.

The Claude Chrome extension had a 50% drop in share, going from 7% to 3.5%, though it had a 30% increase in number of requests. Google’s newly released Gemini agent (introduced Oct. 8, per HUMAN) came in at No. 8 with 0.8%. xAI’s Grok Agent was newly introduced to the top 10 at No. 9 with 0.7%.

In a recent development, genspark’s browser-based agent dropped off the top 10 list entirely; Perplexity’s Comet agent accounted for 41% of all agent requests in August but this figure declined to only 9.4% in September and then further to only 3.6% by October. Comet was also the only top-10 agent that experienced a drop-off in request volume during October, with a decline of approximately 30% since August. In addition, OpenAI discontinued its standalone ChatGPT Atlas browser in August.

The report attributes this downward trend to customers selecting an agent based on either their familiarity with the platform or having used another product offered by the same firm.

In October, 85% of all agent requests in the report were directed toward product and search pages. This represents an increase over the previous month’s percentage when such requests totaled 81%. During the same period, requests made to checkout and payment pages decreased from 2.4% of the total to 1.9%.

According to the report, agents “still browse far more than they buy” but the number of requests making their way to checkout has been increasing at a rapid pace. The report’s page categorizations represent where a request ended up rather than what action was being taken, so a request arriving on a checkout page does not signify an order had been placed.

Industry observers note that ecommerce websites generated a stable share of approximately 60% of agent requests during this period, and travel was the second highest category, according to the report. Media generated the third largest portion among all categories tracked, marking the first time in this series that travel websites have outperformed media.

Industry observers note that HUMAN uses a combination of behavioral data along with user-agent strings and, when available, publisher-level integration to determine what is agent generated, and it excludes crawler activity. The report claims AgenticTrust has identified and verified Muse using HUMAN’s own proprietary research and digital signature validation. The report does not provide further breakdown on the percentage of Muse detected through each method.

In Meta’s engineering post on Muse, the firm says Muse’s browsing “will appear as your activity” to the sites it visits.

Sources indicate that muse transferred its Web Bot Auth signatures from Meta’s key directory (meta.com) to its own (muse.ai) between Nov. 7 and Nov. 9, according to DataDome’s reporting on Nov. 11. Web Bot Auth allows agents to identify themselves by signing the request they are sending to a site, allowing the receiving site to verify the identity of who is making the request. At the time of my review on Nov. 13, the muse.ai key directory was active.

As of Nov. 10, half of Muse’s requests on DataDome’s network were being made without being signed, so there would be no signature to verify the source of the request. According to DataDome, sites that verify signatures and only accept those based on meta.com will now see Muse’s requests as having no verification. Both DataDome and HUMAN sell bot and agent identification services.

Sources indicate that for ecommerce and travel teams, HUMAN’s October report narrows down whose agents are sending most agent requests. In HUMAN’s data, two companies’ agents account for nearly nine in ten.

As Slobodan Manic wrote for SEJ in October, an agent like Muse gives robots.txt no name to match, so the decision about letting it in moves to bot protection. A bot rule that verifies signatures now needs Muse’s muse.ai directory, and in DataDome’s Nov. 10 count, about half of Muse’s requests carried no signature to check.

HUMAN’s report also says analytics tools on most sites can’t tell AI agents from human visitors. Muse and OpenAI’s three agents make a short list to raise with whoever runs bot protection before Black Friday.

The thing to watch is whether more of Muse’s requests start arriving signed. HUMAN says next month’s report will show how agents behaved over Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

Right now, if you don’t want your site to be scraped by AI companies, you have to block each organization’s crawlers individually. On Friday, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft said they would support a common robots.txt signal that, per OpenAI, “makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.”.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic engineer Kevin Kelley proposed the common signal as part of work for the Internet Engineering Task Force, and Anthropic is already supporting it. OpenAI says it will do so “in the coming months,” and Google and Microsoft say they’ll do so next year.

Meta VP of communications Andy Stone called the common signal “an important step,” writing in a tweet that the company supports “publishers’ ability to express preferences about how their content is used for foundational generative AI training.” Meta is under scrutiny for proposed commercial terms that would allow broad scraping; last week, it agreed to delay implementation of those terms.

We’ve got a big and expansive indicates group, and I referred to that in my prepared remarks, where we’re putting a lot of resource and energy into a growing stable of shows that are getting more and more cultural resonance.

    We also continue to have a massive effort on visual investigations, which we’ve referred to in prior quarters and in prepared remarks. I referred today in my prepared remarks to a very big effort in the development of short-form video. We’ve talked about that pretty extensively, so a lot of reporter video. Then also now, we’re rolling out more assertively some short-form video franchises, like the one I mentioned from our fashion critic, Vanessa Friedman. We’ve got another one coming from one of the hosts of The Daily. All that, I would just say, reflects a sort of big effort to sort of harness the investment we’ve already made in extraordinary journalists and journalism and put it into new forms.

    I think you’ve heard both [EVP and CFO Will Bardeen] and I talk about this is a key area of investment, and we expect it to drive more engagement, and ultimately, over time, we expect that to enhance our monetization.

    United Lets Search Engines Index Its Site, Makes AI Agents Ask First via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (998 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • United Airlines’ website terms, updated Nov.
    • Sources indicate that the changes came with United’s announcement that it is restricting unauthorized third-party AI agents on its own platforms and through travel agencies and booking sites.
    • For those on SEO and ecommerce teams who have created their own rules for AI agents, the airline’s rules are an example of what a major company has done.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    United Airlines’ website terms, updated Nov. 11, allow search engines to index its public pages. However, any AI agent that searches, books, or makes purchases on united.com or in its app needs written permission. The terms also bar anyone from using fares, schedules, availability, pricing or other data from United’s site or app to “train, fine-tune, ground, evaluate, or otherwise develop” an AI model.

    Sources indicate that the changes came with United’s announcement that it is restricting unauthorized third-party AI agents on its own platforms and through travel agencies and booking sites. The airline updated its contract of carriage (the passenger agreement that comes with buying a ticket) on the same day.

    For those on SEO and ecommerce teams who have created their own rules for AI agents, the airline’s rules are an example of what a major company has done. The rules for the AI agents can be found in both the terms and conditions and the contract. As of Nov. 14, United’s robots.txt file named no crawlers or agents for any AI.

    Industry observers note that the announcement from United notes that sharing account login credentials with an outside third-party AI assistant can expose customers’ sensitive information. Furthermore, according to the announcement, there are potential risks of “unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles.” In addition to these risks, automated actions by the AI assistant may violate Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and Department of Transportation (DOT) regulations. United points to check-in as an example, saying it requires a person to acknowledge that their bags hold no banned items like explosives.

    United’s FAQ on its Digital Trust Center calls any AI agent, bot, browser extension or browser feature unauthorized if it searches, books, buys, manages or collects information on united.com or the United app without United’s permission. Using AI to research and proposal a trip is allowed as long as the tool doesn’t access united.com or the app.

    In a recent development, united doesn’t work with any third-party AI agents yet, according to the FAQ, and bookings that agents made before Nov. 11 won’t be canceled.

    In The Wall Street Journal’s report, CEO Scott Kirby said at an event in Chicago, “I don’t want to create another middleman.”.

    United’s terms of service define an Automated Agent as any software, service or feature that, with full or partial autonomy, searches, books, buys or manages items on the United website or app, or extracts or copies data from those websites or apps. This includes AI assistants, bots, scrapers, browser extensions and features built into browsers or apps, even if a person supervises or approves the actions of the Automated Agent.

    No Automated Agent shall be permitted to access United’s site or app without prior written permission from United, and United reserves the right to block or impede an Automated Agent at any time, regardless of who operates it (the user, a third party or an artificial intelligence firm).

    One of the uses United’s terms of service bar for data pulled from its site or app is grounding, which involves an AI system pulling in outside content to build a response.

    Search engines that index the public pages of united.com are exempt under the terms of service. The terms of service also exempt assistive technology and standard browsers used by a person. However, built-in agent features of a browser are not exempt. Additionally, the terms of service do not address how they treat answers created by AI systems from search engines’ indexes.

    Use of an Automated Agent on United’s site results in acceptance of the agreement by the user, whoever runs the agent and the person for whom the agent acts. In September, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agent based on its Conditions of Use, which bind the shopper rather than Meta, as Slobodan Manic reported for SEJ. eBay has added “buy-for-me agents, LLM-driven bots” to its User Agreement‘s list of automated tools that need eBay’s permission, in an patch it posted in January.

    The highlighted excerpts below show United’s permission requirement and its search-indexing exception.

    The contract of carriage uses its own term “AI Agent” to describe all computer-based applications (software) utilized on behalf of a traveler or other individuals, to locate, research, book, purchase or otherwise manage any offer from or through United, regardless of whether an individual is monitoring or approving such activity. Examples include assistant capabilities built into social media, messaging or search platforms, browsers utilizing AI capabilities, stand-alone AI-enabled agents, and third-party AI assistants connected to United via some type of interface provided by a travel agency or other intermediary.

    It has been revealed that rule 6.J.6 adds using AI agents to “make, modify or service a Ticket,” or to buy any service or product, to the contract’s prohibited practices, next to hidden-city and throwaway ticketing. Rule 5.H lists bookings that AI agents made, changed or serviced among the improper bookings United will cancel without notice.

    Industry observers note that according to the FAQ, travel agencies and booking platforms aren’t permitted to use third-party AI agents to search for, book, or manage United travel on behalf of customers. Agencies also need to get United’s permission before using their own third-party AI tools.

    United’s terms separate search indexing from AI agent access, and none of it depends on robots.txt. Personal agents like Muse publish no user agent for a robots.txt rule to name, as Manic wrote in October. Reviewing your robots.txt, terms, and bot protection together can help you see whether they’re aligned on what an AI agent is allowed to do on your site.

    It has been revealed that united notes it will keep reviewing how AI assistants work with its services and will enhancement its FAQ if it starts working with third-party agents. United’s release, FAQ, terms and contract don’t say how it detects an agent, so watch how the rules are enforced for travel agencies and agent makers, and whether other airlines write similar rules.

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories.’”.

    Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals.

    It has been revealed that but not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution. Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor Lucia Torres has found. Turning that kind of journalism into something people stop scrolling for isn’t easy.

    “Generally mass audiences are less interested in environmental content on YouTube [and] Instagram,” Torres noted. “We have to compete with recipes, music videos, etc.”.

    Mongabay publishes around 150 to 200 videos a year with a team of four full-time and one half-time producers. These include short vertical videos on YouTube Shorts and Instagram; evergreen explainers around “complex enviro-problems”; twice-monthly features; and lengthy investigations or short documentaries.

    It has been revealed that to reach new audiences with its environmental journalism, Mongabay started experimenting with behind-the-scenes reels in late 2024. At the time, Mongabay’s Instagram reels averaged 2,000 to 3,000 views. Torres noted she was inspired by behind-the-scenes videos from National Geographic, The New York Times, ProPublica, and contributing creator Izzy Sasada. An early behind-the-scenes video — on pollution from those shrimp farms — drew about 14,000 views. Additional videos from California and Indonesia each got about 6,000 views. Mongabay started to dive deeper with videos that featured sources and reporters filming from the field.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Recent findings suggest that from the initial tests, it became clear to Torres that the best-performing videos were ones with behind-the-scenes footage from investigations or collaborations. Putting reporters on camera — in the field or at their desks — worked.

    “The content [on platforms like Instagram] is dominated now by individual content creators,” mentioned Torres, who is currently a Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. She said Mongabay is “still figuring out how we can create personalities or creators within the organization that represent what Mongabay does — that are good journalists but also good at talking in front of the camera.”.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Industry observers note that another successful example came with Mongabay’s investigation into vanishing forests in Liberia. The piece ran as a long-form article, a lengthy YouTube video, and a behind-the-scenes short.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Mongabay now intends its multimedia packages for big investigative stories from the beginning. “They require cross-team, high-level collaborations,” Torres stated. “You really have to think about all the elements you are going to use before starting production so when you’re in the field you get everything you need.”.

    Not everything has panned out. Last year, Mongabay tried a data visualization series on climate data. It didn’t work. The lessons for the newsroom went beyond video.

    In a recent development, “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories,’” Torres said. “The simple mention of ‘climate’ scares them away.”.

    CEO and founder Rhett Butler has seen the same thing across Mongabay’s journalism.

    “We’re seeing strong evidence that doomer stories are resonating less with our audiences,” he said. “Climate stories — especially those focused on disasters or the climate emergency — tend to garner less interest than other topics.” The ones that do well, he added, have “an ecosystem or wildlife angle, give readers a sense of agency, or present a solution.”.

    Mongabay has responded by introducing more projects and series focused on solutions journalism, like Indigenous-led conservation, agroecology, and conservation technology.

    In a recent development, RELATED ARTICLEAudience editors offer advice for “dispiriting” times in social and searchSarah ScireJanuary 16, 2025“We’ve also been sharing data with the newsroom about which kinds of framing are reaching more people right now, so writers and editors can consider whether they might want to incorporate how people are responding to problems into their stories,” Butler said. “But we aren’t overly prescriptive, so ultimately it’s up to editors and writers how they use this information.”.

    Sources indicate that looking at the 3,422 articles published between June 1, 2025 and August 31, 2026, Butler found that the median story featuring hope or a solution got 41% more traffic than articles that only described the crisis or threat. (Articles classified as being about an “action confronting a threat” got 43% more.).

    Recent findings suggest that today, 71% of the 100 most-read stories on Mongabay’s English-language site can be classified as “hope / solution / agency” or “action confronting a threat,” Butler remarked. Only 21% were “doom only.”.

    It has been revealed that the video team has done something similar. The environmental newsroom’s short series Stranger Creatures leads with “the wonder of wild creatures first,” Torres noted. The conservation or endangered species angle follows.

    Sources indicate that “We’ve stopped framing stories as a climate problem, and started framing stories from a solutions-oriented, action-driven perspective, community-first, or fun-stuff first,” Torres mentioned. “Climate is implicit now in the stories.”.

    Sources indicate that what video won’t be, at least for now, is a revenue generator. Almost all of Mongabay’s revenue comes from contributions and grants, according to its annual report. (Events, licensing, and advertising “are insignificant at this point,” Butler said.).

    According to recent reports, “I’m not bullish on video becoming a material source of revenue for Mongabay, given how the space has evolved and our position in it,” Butler mentioned. “Ten years ago I was a lot more optimistic on that front.”.

    Part of the problem, he stated, is incentives. “Building a video strategy around advertising creates an incentive to prioritize views, which may not align with our broader organizational emphasis on impact,” Butler said. “The stories that attract the largest audiences aren’t necessarily those most likely to inform decisions or prompt action.”.

    Recent findings suggest that you’ll work closely with Partner Solutions Architects and Partner Engineers at Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable, helping us proactively identify builder problems where Supabase is the right solution and closing the gap between partner intent and real developer outcomes. This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions of AI-native apps and agents.

    In this role, you’ll focus on three core pillars:.

    Build deep relationships with Technical counterparts at Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable, focusing initially on defined use cases and agent/app-migration motions.

    Develop and deliver technical workshops, training materials, and enablement content to give partner SAs the fluency to position Supabase.

    Create demos, integration guides, and reference architectures that make Supabase’s fit with Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable immediately legible.

    Partner with SAs at these companies on active opportunities to move deals forward and feeding technical pipeline intelligence back to the alliance lead.

    Resolve blockers for partner SAs working on Supabase implementations to maintain their credibility with the builders they support.

    Troubleshoot complex integration scenarios and turn solutions into reusable assets.

    Maintain a close feedback loop with Supabase product and engineering teams to ensure technical guidance reflects the latest platform capabilities.

    Measure success through co-sell opportunities sourced, influenced deals, and SA enablement metrics across the Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable partnerships.

    Write technical blog posts and case studies that demonstrate real-world Supabase implementations built on Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable.

    Represent Supabase at conferences, meetups, and partner-sponsored events (e.g. Anthropic and OpenAI dev days, Vercel Ship, Lovable community events).

    Develop video content and interactive learning experiences to reduce the "time-to-fluency" for partner SAs.

    In a recent development, have 5+ years of experience in technical roles with deep hands-on experience building on modern AI infrastructure. Previous experience working at Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, Lovable (or a similar AI builder platform) or as a partner to one is required.

    Understand how partner SAs at AI builder platforms are incentivized, how they make recommendations, and how the partner ecosystem influences developer decisions.

    Communicate clearly across both technical and non-technical audiences, explaining complex concepts with ease.

    Have a strong technical foundation in PostgreSQL, APIs, and modern development frameworks like React and Next.js, plus fluency with AI/agent tooling (LLM APIs, MCP, agent frameworks).

    Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving swiftly to build a playbook from scratch.

    Are energized by solving real-world problems for developers building the next generation of AI-native products.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    In a recent development, every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

    Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    Sources indicate that we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    College football already has an Orange Bowl, a Peach Bowl, and a Citrus Bowl, so on its face, there’s nothing outlandish about the concept of an Onion Bowl.

    But this matchup wouldn’t be titled to evoke some locale’s bumper crop, à la the Famous Idaho Potato Bowl. Instead it would market “America’s Finest News Source,” The Onion. (Today’s top headlines: Bain Capital Acquires Tibetan Buddhism For $35 Million; Abdul El-Sayed Makes History As First Physically Healthy Senator; Chuck Schumer Delivers Victory Speech To Previously Enthusiastic Crowd.).

    On Thursday morning, Onion CEO (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Ben Collins announced the publication’s quest to buy naming rights for a bowl game, both on Bluesky and on the podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out:.

    The Onion is extremely close to buying an honest-to-goodness, Division 1 college football bowl series bowl game.

    Yes, we're trying to pull off The Onion Bowl.

    A few days before Christmas, potentially in Texas.

    Industry observers note that but we've already been banned once. And we need your help.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:32 AM.

    For those unfamiliar, American college football seasons traditionally end with a few dozen bowl games, scattered around the country (and occasionally outside it). Nearly all of these games sell naming rights to one firm or another, leading to fun combinations like the Poulan Weed Eater Independence Bowl, the TaxSlayer.com Gator Bowl, and the Union Home Mortgage Gasparilla Bowl. Collins wants to buy the rights to one of the several bowl games that are still without a sponsor for their games next month.

    This absurdity — though no more absurd, I suppose, than the Snoop Dogg Arizona Bowl presented by Gin & Juice by Dre and Snoop — serves as the excellent marketing hook to get people to buy a $75/year print subscription, a major driver of The Onion’s revenue.

    Indeed, only three U.S. newspapers have a daily print circulation over 100,000 — The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, and the New York Post; The Washington Post and USA Today have already fallen below that line. (At the risk of being pedantic, though, The Onion appears in print monthly, not daily, making it a bit of an apples-to-oranges comparison. Also, The Onion gets to make up its stories.).

    Recent findings suggest that collins states The Onion actually got quite close to buying the naming rights to the New Orleans Bowl, which last year lost its longtime naming sponsor, the…Ohio-based freight-shipping concern R+L Carriers? The Onion was prepared to pay “mid six figures.” But the organization that runs the bowl, the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation, apparently remarked no deep into the process, a move Collins attributed to “politics.” (I reached out to the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation for comment — a sentence I did not expect to type today — but did not hear back.).

    So the guys who sell bowl games ushered us to what we thought was a pretty good fit: The Latest Orleans Bowl.

    I love New Orleans. I love having crawfish out of the back of a pickup truck at 3 a.m. The game would've been in the Superdome two days before Christmas. Good fit! Right? Right???

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:38 AM.

    Then the folks who run the Latest Orleans Bowl, a commission that includes representatives of the city and state of Louisiana, found out our plans to highlight our mascot:.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:39 AM.

    Despite getting all approvals from ESPN and scraping together the cash, right as we were about to sign the paper work to put The Onion Sports Bowl in Fresh Orleans, their state-funded commission called us and noted it straight up: "No.".

    We asked why. They said politics. And the Sickos Guy.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:40 AM.

    While the Latest Orleans Bowl might be out, several currently-brand-free possibilities remain, including the Frisco Bowl in newly blue Texas — the state also home to The Onion’s rival to the death, Alex Jones.

    Core Update, ChatGPT Business Hub & AI Mode’s Latest Model – SEO Pulse via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Welcome to the week’s Pulse: what’s changing affects how you read ranking movement, which data ChatGPT will report back to businesses, and how larger sites believe search traffic will perform.
    • This week saw Google announce its core update while it also changed the default model that is used by AI Mode.
    • Google started rolling out the November 2026 core update on Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to the week’s Pulse: what’s changing affects how you read ranking movement, which data ChatGPT will report back to businesses, and how larger sites believe search traffic will perform.

    This week saw Google announce its core update while it also changed the default model that is used by AI Mode. OpenAI declared that Business Hub is available in beta, and three company earnings calls dealt with decreasing search referral numbers and paid crawl hints.

    Here’s what matters for you and your work.

    Google started rolling out the November 2026 core update on Nov. 10.

    Key facts: This is the third Search core revision of the year. According to the Search Status Dashboard, the update “applies globally and to all languages”. Per the dashboard, the update “may take up to 2 weeks to complete”. At 10:06 a.m. PT on Nov. 10 the rollout had just begun and as of Nov. 12, the update was still in progress. Google’s Search Central team also referred to the update as “a regular update” on their LinkedIn page.

    Google advises waiting at least a full week after a core revision has rolled out, then trying to compare your Search Console data from that week (the week after rollout) to the week prior to when the rollout began. Going by Google’s estimate of two weeks, the first full week after rollout would include U.S. Thanksgiving Day, Black Friday and Cyber Monday, so online retailers making this comparison would be comparing their holiday traffic to their average non-holiday week.

    Read our full coverage: Google’s November 2026 Core Patch Starts Rolling Out.

    Industry observers note that openAI opened Business Hub in beta on Nov. 10, letting businesses claim their ChatGPT profiles and see how often ChatGPT mentions them and sends clicks to their websites.

    Sources indicate that key facts: Any eligible business located where ChatGPT is available can claim its business, according to OpenAI’s announcement. Once the claim and identity verification are approved, Insights show aggregated mentions, website clicks and discovery topics for the past 28 days. OpenAI’s setup guide says a mention for an online business counts when ChatGPT references the business’s website, and the brand name alone doesn’t count. Vahan Petrosyan, SEJ’s director of technology, submitted Search Engine Journal and reported 353,356 mentions and 2,663 website clicks from Oct. 14 to Nov. 10.

    For an online business, OpenAI counts in Business Hub’s Insights how many times a reference is made to this business by ChatGPT and how many clicks are generated from those references. A recorded click isn’t a confirmed visit, so those clicks are the numbers to put next to the number of referrals you see in your analytics for the last 28 days. The setup guide also says that a blank metric doesn’t always mean there was no activity, and simply claiming a business will not guarantee increased visibility within ChatGPT’s responses.

    Read our full coverage: How to Submit Your Website to ChatGPT Business Hub.

    Google made Gemini 4 Hydrogen the default model in AI Mode on Nov. 12 and is using it for some AI Overview questions too.

    Key facts: Robby Stein, Vice President of Product at Google Search posted the announcement about the change on an X thread and stated Hydrogen is “being used for your hardest questions in AI Overviews”. Google’s Search post states the model is available everywhere in Search to everyone, and that it has better query fan out, connecting customers to “a broader range of helpful links than before”. The Search post and the thread do not give link numbers, and the thread did not say what would be considered the hardest AI Overview questions.

    According to recent reports, citation tracking for AI Mode and AI Overviews in November now spans a model change on Nov. 12, two days after the core patch began. Logging both dates makes it easier to compare what happened before and after each one, while your citation and referral numbers can help you assess Google’s claim of a broader range of links for your site.

    Read our full coverage: Google Makes Gemini 4 Hydrogen The Default Model In AI Mode.

    It has been revealed that ziff Davis CEO Vivek Shah said on the company’s third-quarter call that it is “not planning on a search recovery”. Tripadvisor CFO Mike Noonan said on his company’s call that SEO will still be a headwind to growth in 2027.

    Key facts: Shah said organic Google referrals to Ziff Davis properties fell about 37% year over year in the quarter. He also put about 2.7 billion AI Overview and AI Mode impressions in Search Console for the quarter at nearly 10 times “the clicks those same sites received from Google Search”. Tripadvisor took a $369.5 million non-cash goodwill impairment on its Hotels and Other segment in the quarter, which its earnings release attributes largely to traffic headwinds from “changes in the search landscape”. Marketing took 48.8% of Tripadvisor’s revenue from continuing operations, up from 43.3% a year earlier, and Noonan tied the rise to a move from free to paid channels.

    Shah’s comparison of the number of AI feature impressions versus the overall clicks in Google Search does not represent an AI click-through rate, since Search Console counts clicks on those features (AI Overview and AI Mode) inside the overall total. Similar comparisons are available to sites that have access to the generative AI report, as they too may be able to measure these types of ratios based upon their own data. On the Tripadvisor side, the planning number is marketing’s share of revenue, which the company connects to its move from free search traffic to paid channels.

    Read our full coverage: Ziff Davis CEO: ‘Not Planning On A Search Recovery’ and Tripadvisor Notes SEO Will Still Weigh On Growth In 2027.

    Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince said on the tech giant’s third-quarter call that OpenAI is paying for hints that tell its crawler when web pages change.

    Key facts: Prince said the quarter brought the manufacturer’s first revenue from Act 4, its name for products aimed at a fresh business model for the internet, with OpenAI’s payments as one example. On the call, neither that revenue nor OpenAI’s payments came with a figure. For customers that want more traffic from AI agents, he called Cloudflare’s help “sort of the new version of SEO”. He also expects some form of micropayments, with sites possibly charging agents less when the agents explain why they’re visiting.

    Industry observers note that the Act 4 payment Prince referred to was paid to Cloudflare for improving the efficiency of OpenAI’s web crawling, and the call had no discussion about sharing revenue with owners of the sites providing these hints. Welcoming crawlers or blocking them are options existing Cloudflare customers have for each individual crawler (AI Crawl Control exists on every blueprint).

    Read our full coverage: Cloudflare CEO Likens AI Agent Optimization To A Latest Version Of SEO.

    Industry observers note that several of the AI search metrics reported this week were defined by the platforms themselves; each platform’s metric is based on that platform’s specific definition. For example, Business Hub uses OpenAI’s definitions to determine how many mentions exist, while Shah’s comparison puts the AI impressions (as defined by Google Search Console) next to all of Google Search clicks. Google described a broader range of links for Hydrogen but did not provide an actual count. Cloudflare acknowledged that OpenAI does pay for crawl hints, but it did not give the dollar amount. Both Ziff Davis and Tripadvisor are already building their strategies around reduced amounts of free search traffic. Any report built on these numbers should carry the platform’s definition next to each one, and the dates of the core update and the Hydrogen switch belong in your own log.

    “I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, ‘OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.’”.

    The data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

    For Nikita Redkar, a major part of filming a video is putting together an outfit.

    Industry observers note that in a July video about youth-led protests in India, the 33-year-old is walking around Latest York City explaining how movements grow when people with opposing views come together on the things they do agree on. She’s wearing a white tube top and black jeans with sunglasses holding her hair back, along with a matching gold necklace and earrings that look like soda can tabs. You can’t see her shoes, but they clack enough for you to know she’s wearing a heel.

    In another about comedian Shane Gillis’s Saturday Night Live monologue in which he called women “whores” for wearing shorts to the gym, she’s seated on the floor of her living room wearing a black silk velvet top with a pink faux-fur collar and sleeve cuffs. In the style of a Get Ready With Me video, she explains how 2000s comedy and pop culture entrenched misogynistic ideas of gender roles while applying her makeup.

    A full-time news creator who mostly focuses on American politics and culture through a leftist and feminist lens, Redkar calls herself a “professor at Bimbo University.” The girliness is the point, she told me.

    Recent findings suggest that “I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice these parts of yourself to be taken seriously,” Redkar said. “You should be taken seriously no matter what.”.

    It has been revealed that redkar and I chatted in October about how she does her job, leaning into her femininity to explain the news, and what her relationship with social media is like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

    Sources indicate that hanaa’ Tameez: How did you start creating news videos? Nikita Redkar: I started in 2022, kind of accidentally. I did standup comedy for five years before the pandemic. I was always doing political humor. I took many political science classes in college, I wrote for the college newspaper, and I always had an interest in politics. In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent. I tried that formula again a couple weeks later…about NATO and fears of World War III. I explained exactly what would be affected. I noted there’s not going to be a world war, but things are going to get really expensive, which happened. I also used a girly friendship metaphor for that video. That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

It makes the present a little less daunting when you study historical cycles and realize that people 100 years ago dealt with [similar things to what we’re going through now]. How did they come out of that?

    Tameez: How do you define your niche and how did you get there? Redkar: My niche is educational. Bimbo University is a place where anyone can start no matter where they are [in their political education]. My audience [ranges from] people who are just getting into politics to people who maybe were triggered by a specific event in the news to start paying more attention to it. I feel like leftist content creators all operate on a spectrum. You have people who are getting really deep into Marxist theory, for example, and things like geopolitics. I’m at the beginning. I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, “OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.”.

    It has been revealed that redkar: On Mondays, I have a researcher and we go through the topics that people are talking about on social media. We pull up some news sites and see what the big stories are, and we leave some room for breaking news throughout the week.

    Industry observers note that my week is [split] between videos [on topics] that the general public is talking about, and videos that are just interesting to me. That’s how I stay sane in this business. I’m lucky to have the flexibility of doing that. My researcher combs through news sites and research papers and compiles all that information for me, then I put together a script.

    Redkar: It’s definitely my favorite color, but it’s like the chicken and the egg — I don’t know if I liked it before I was doing this.

    In a recent development, I pick whatever outfit I feel cute in. In getting ready with me videos, I start with a completely bare face, so at least the outfit has to be giving a little bit.

    Industry observers note that tameez: Tell me about the Get Ready with Me videos. How do you decide what’s a GRWM and what’s a walking video?

    Redkar: It’s like: What am I comfortable screaming out in the streets versus what do I need to keep at home? Some topics require more seriousness; if it does, I can do the GRWM for that. But if it’s something [less serious], I can be walking my dog or have on some ridiculous outfit.

    Redkar: If I get a fact wrong, I’ll do a follow-up video. It’s rare that I’ve gotten a fact wrong because between me and my researcher, that’s two levels of checks before something hits the internet.

    Industry observers note that for one video, I didn’t factually get it wrong, but I should have included more of the story. It was about the Ugandan dictator Idi Amin and how Indians were expelled from Uganda, which is kind of how we got both Zohran Mamdani and Charli XCX [living in the U.S.], because both of their parents were part of the group that was expelled. I disregarded the racism that local Ugandans faced because of the Indians. I just focused on the expulsion and I framed Indians as the victims.

    A lot of people in the comments were like, “Hey, like, you really should have mentioned this other part too.” I just deleted that video, because I didn’t want this to spread and only give half of the story.

    Sources indicate that redkar: My favorite video in recent memory was about girls on the first date, how we’re all so vigilant these days about dating men. I had so much fun doing it because I was talking about how life is affected by politics, instead of just politics. I think that video did really well because a lot of people connected to it.

    In a recent development, last year I did a video that I called “How we went from Brat Summer to Hitler Winter” and talked about the hedonism of the 2024 summer and the fascism that followed. I related it to the Roaring 20s transitioning to the Great Depression to the World War. I incorporated a lot of pop culture [references].

I thought it was so interesting and timely, but it did not do well at all. The problem with content creation is sometimes you can’t tell if people didn’t like a video or if you’re being shadow banned.

    In a recent development, redkar: I really love Liz Plank. She’s @feministabulous on Instagram. I love her coverage and how she leans into current conversations in pop culture.

    Recent findings suggest that I really like Charles McBryde. He’s not talking about just news — he’s very foreign policy-focused as well.

    @MissEatingGood on Instagram is a great explainer of what’s going on and the historical context.

    Recent findings suggest that redkar: Just finding ways to work together. I think there is so much benefit in that. I know countless creators who take a journalist’s article and dissect it down. Maybe [the journalists] should be the ones doing that.

    I would happily pair up with journalists and teach them the ins and outs of content creation and how to make a short-form video article that’s also attention-grabbing. That’s just the reality; people are on social media, everyone’s attention span is shot, which sucks. We could try to fix that, but at this moment, we’re not fixing it. It’s really helpful to go on social media and talk [about your reporting] because journalists work hard on their articles.

    Creators [should] take more time. We rush way too much. It’s not our fault, because these platforms reward you for making content more frequently and punish you if you take a few days off. [Not rushing] sucks, but what can you do? It’s better than putting incorrect, or rushed, or incomplete information out there.

    Industry observers note that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Nearly there — check your email.

    In a recent development, we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    “We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right.”.

    Meta has indefinitely delayed its proposed commercial terms of service, which would have permitted the organization to scrape the websites of Meta Business account owners.

    It has been revealed that on Thursday, the company took down the preview link to the proposed terms and published an enhancement to its Business Help Center that reads: “We recently shared that we were updating the Meta Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms. These updates are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026. We are continuing to consult with stakeholders and will provide a further update when we have more to share. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect.”.

    Meta — which owns Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — has repeatedly pushed back the terms’ effective date since Nieman Lab first reported on them on October 15. The terms were first set to take effect on October 30, sparking global outcry among news publishers, politicians, and trade organizations. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” On October 23, Meta moved the effective date back by three weeks to November 20.

    Last week, Meta pledged to consult news publishers and industry leaders ahead of putting new commercial terms into effect.

    In a recent development, “We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms upgrade. We care deeply about our partners and do not strategy to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted on October 28. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms.”.

    It has been revealed that since then, courts in Norway and Brazil have issued preliminary injunctions to block the terms from taking effect as a result of lawsuits filed by media organizations in both countries. The United Kingdom’s Competition and Markets Authority has opened a formal investigation into Meta, examining whether the manufacturer was “abusing a dominant position by imposing exploitative terms on publishers and advertisers.”.

    In the United States, the proposed terms stoked bipartisan concern. At the end of October, Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sent letters to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg asking him to withdraw the terms.

    Tech Report: YouTube’s Clips Tool Turns Podcast Episodes Into Shorts via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that youTube has expanded the video clips tool in YouTube Studio to Shorts, so creators can turn segments of long-form videos, such as podcast episodes, into vertical Shorts.
    • In an April post, YouTube mentioned it would be “rolling out Video Clips to Shorts” later in the year.
    • The help page explains that each Short created using this tool has the original video as its related video.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that youTube has expanded the video clips tool in YouTube Studio to Shorts, so creators can turn segments of long-form videos, such as podcast episodes, into vertical Shorts. TeamYouTube revealed the change Nov. 12 in a YouTube Help Community post aimed at podcast creators.

    In an April post, YouTube mentioned it would be “rolling out Video Clips to Shorts” later in the year. The tool’s help page has described the Shorts option since at least Sept. 10, according to an Internet Archive capture.

    The help page explains that each Short created using this tool has the original video as its related video. A clickable link of the source video will be located underneath the channel handle. However, if the Short is either private, unlisted or Made for Kids, then the tool won’t add the link.

    The automatic link gives teams with a video podcast or webinar series a way to send viewers from a Short back to the whole episode.

    When they are in YouTube Studio, creators open one of their pre-existing long-form videos. On the left-hand side of the screen is a list of options including Clips and Shorts. If they choose Short, they have two ways to create the Short.

    Here’s an example from YouTube’s demo showing the Short creation option in Studio.

    They can enter timestamps into the timeline editor. Alternatively, they may select some text in their video’s transcript to create the Short.

    According to recent reports, where available, the left-hand panel also reveals AI-powered suggestions and an outline of the transcript that AI generates. YouTube’s post states it picks “moments in your episode that can be watched independently” so creators can review and edit them.

    The selection screen places suggested Shorts beside the transcript and the original video.

    The post describes how a widescreen episode becomes a Short:.

    “For Shorts, your 16:9 podcast episode will be transformed into a verticalized video, keeping the most notable parts of the video in the frame.”.

    The help page says captions are added automatically where available, and creators can change their color, font, styling and position or turn them off.

    Here’s the vertical preview from the same demo, with captions and a Create draft button.

    In a recent development, for standard video clips, which the tool still makes, the help page’s tip is to add a link to the source video in the clip’s description. YouTube also recommends keeping only full episodes in podcast playlists.

    YouTube’s help page for the clips tool lists AI-powered suggestions and outlines for creators in Brazil, Canada, France, Germany, India, Mexico, South Korea, Spain, the U.K. and the U.S. The supported languages are English, French, German, Hindi, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish.

    In an April capture, the page limited suggestions to English-language videos in a podcast playlist in the U.S. and Canada. The current page doesn’t mention podcast playlists for suggestions.

    On Oct. 1, YouTube stated it would reduce the reach of channels that mainly aggregate or re-upload other creators’ clips without significant changes. In my coverage, I wrote that YouTube’s video on the change didn’t discuss creators cutting Shorts from their own long-form videos.

    Unless it’s private, unlisted, or Made for Kids, a Short created with the clips tool will automatically link to its full-length episode. When you create a Short on another platform and upload it yourself to YouTube, YouTube’s related video help page has you add that link manually after uploading. To do this requires advanced feature access.

    Sources indicate that beyond stating that creators won’t be penalized for using their own content in a clip or Short, the help page’s note didn’t address recommendations, which was specifically what the Oct. 1 Shorts changes were about.

    Recent findings suggest that according to YouTube’s post, they are at the moment working to expand the AI suggestion system to more of their creators in the near future but do not include specific countries, languages, nor time frames. If you have a YouTube channel located outside of the 10-country limit or the seven-language limit included on the help page, then this will be the list to reference prior to developing a clipping routine based on suggested content.

    In a recent development, liveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing. Our platform gives developers everything they need to build, test, deploy, scale, and observe agents in production. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice AI applications for OpenAI, xAI, Salesforce, Coursera, Spotify, and thousands of others, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

    Most product designers want to design for everyone. This role is for someone who'd rather design for one very specific, very opinionated person: the developer at 2am trying to figure out why their voice agent just failed a call. You'll design the tools developers use to test, evaluate and debug AI agents — a category that's still being invented, with no established patterns to copy. If dense data, real-time systems and reading a stack trace sound more fun than intimidating, keep reading.

    You'll thrive as a Senior Product Designer if you:.

    are obsessed with making the best product for our customers.

    are known as the go-to person for tackling tough problems.

    work hard and can build and ship fast.

    are focused on polish, detail and quality.

    are a fast learner, frequently picking up latest tips, tricks, and skills.

    The best way to impress us is with thoughtful ways you'd implement LiveKit, and potentially tinkering with it 😊.

    Own the design of how developers test, evaluate and observe their agents — simulations, evals, logs and agent insights.

    Turn complex, real-time data into interfaces that are easy to scan, understand and act on.

    Design latest interaction patterns for AI-native workflows, where agents generate the first draft and humans adjust it.

    Prototype in code and work hand-in-hand with engineers to ship polished work.

    Contribute patterns to our design system for dense, debugging-oriented surfaces.

    You've shipped design work for developer tools, observability or data-heavy products.

    You have strong data-visualization instincts and know when a chart beats a table (and when it doesn't).

    You're comfortable in code — reading PRs, tweaking Tailwind, building prototypes.

    You earn the trust of deeply technical customers and engineers.

    Experience designing for AI or agent tooling.

    AI tools are already a core part of how you design.

    An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world.

    Contribute to open source alongside world-class engineers.

    Competitive salary and equity package.

    Health, dental, and vision benefits.

    Industry News: Higher Spend Came With Pricier Clicks For 14 B2B Google Advertisers via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1207 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
