    💡 Key Takeaways
    • To determine how much more the same non-branded Google Ads keywords cost 14 B2B advertisers per click during the months of April through September compared to the same time period last year, Grey Matter reviewed their Google Ads Search campaigns.
    • According to the agency report by Grey Matter issued in October, there was an increase of about 21% in cost-per-click (CPC) for the same keywords used by these 14 B2B advertisers, after accounting for changes in their spending, ad position and Quality Score.
    • Andy Hendricks, Grey Matter’s head of search, writes that he wanted to isolate what portion of the overall price change all advertisers experienced versus what portion was due to actions taken by each advertiser individually.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    To determine how much more the same non-branded Google Ads keywords cost 14 B2B advertisers per click during the months of April through September compared to the same time period last year, Grey Matter reviewed their Google Ads Search campaigns.

    According to the agency report by Grey Matter issued in October, there was an increase of about 21% in cost-per-click (CPC) for the same keywords used by these 14 B2B advertisers, after accounting for changes in their spending, ad position and Quality Score. The report gives a likely range of 1% to 44% for that figure. It is based on client Google Ads Search campaign data only, so it does not include Performance Max, Shopping or Display campaigns. All 14 come from the agency’s client base, and its search team runs SEO and paid search programs for B2B companies.

    Andy Hendricks, Grey Matter’s head of search, writes that he wanted to isolate what portion of the overall price change all advertisers experienced versus what portion was due to actions taken by each advertiser individually. Most available CPC benchmarks, such as published averages, do not account for this differentiation and simply provide an overall average CPC.

    In a recent development, grey Matter excluded broad match keywords since the searches they get matched to can change over time; keywords within Maximize Clicks campaigns also do not fit into the analysis. Brand and competitor keywords were also excluded from the overall estimate.

    Recent findings suggest that grey Matter’s analysis is based on tracking 1,349 non-brand keywords, each within one account, for six quarters (April 2025 to September 2026). The year-over-year comparison covers April through September 2026 versus those months a year prior.

    According to recent reports, the headline estimate was derived from a regression model using data from all 14 advertisers in the report which controlled for campaign spend, impression share lost to budget, top-of-page position, and Quality Score. Every advertiser was given equal weight regardless of how much it spends.

    It has been revealed that with no controls applied, the same keywords cost 29% more year over year. Adding the two spend-related controls lowered that to 22%, and position and Quality Score took it to 21%.

    Industry observers note that A second estimation technique used in this analysis was a keyword price index. This measure covered 11 advertisers who had sufficient matching keywords from quarter to quarter.

    The report’s regression ties every 10% increase in campaign spend to about 1.4% higher CPCs, on top of the market increase, or roughly 11% for doubled spend. The report doesn’t give a likely range for that figure.

    Sources indicate that the most extreme case in the sample nearly quadrupled its non-brand Search spend year over year, and its same-keyword CPCs rose 132%. The report says that advertiser’s brand keywords, on a flat budget, rose about 4% year over year in the third quarter.

    Sources indicate that the report sees a correlation between this pattern and automated bidding. It explains that a campaign using a strategy like Maximize Conversions spends a bigger budget by entering auctions it previously skipped, including higher positions, more competitive searches, and pricier times of day.

    It has been revealed that for the 11 advertisers covered by the keyword price index, the overall year-over-year increase in average non-brand CPC was 36%, including the advertisers’ own choices. Of that, 22 points were attributed to the market, and three additional points were attributed to increased spending. There was a three-point deduction due to various types of keyword, match type and bid strategy changes, leaving 14 points that the report’s first three parts don’t explain.

    Grey Matter illustrates that breakdown in the chart below.

    The majority of those 14 points occurred at a few of the advertisers who saw an approximate doubling of their CPCs, which the report said probably represented competition in their respective categories.

    Actual CPC changes ranged from a 30% decrease to a 121% increase. Ten of the 11 paid more for the same keywords, and nine paid more overall. One advertiser kept its spending flat and saw the same keywords rise by 20%. After shifting some of its budget to pricier phrase-match keywords, its overall CPC increased by 40%.

    It has been revealed that with only 14 advertisers in this report, the likely range for the 21% estimate is wide. When the biggest spender is removed from the report’s data, the estimate drops to around 17%, and its likely range of -2% to +40% includes zero. When broad match keywords are included, the estimate rises to around 31%. According to Hendricks, compared with a year ago, that same click most likely costs about 20% more currently, and the true figure “could be meaningfully higher or lower”.

    Industry observers note that the report calls its findings correlation (and not proven causation). There are no references on the report page or in the PDF to the industries or markets of the advertisers used in the report, nor their currency.

    The report doesn’t provide any conversion rate or cost per lead information; so, it can’t show whether these advertisers saw better or worse results along with higher CPCs. Jyll Saskin Gales argued in an April column for Search Engine Journal (SEJ) that under Smart Bidding, a high CPC is often a sign of a healthy account, and that accounts should be evaluated based on CPA or ROAS.

    Alphabet’s third-quarter 10-Q reports that cost-per-click on Google Search & other properties rose 4% year over year in the quarter. Alphabet has defined this metric as click-driven revenue divided by total paid clicks and has cited several factors such as changes in the devices owners access the internet on, geography, advertiser spending, and product mix as variables that affect it.

    The metric is based on paid clicks through Google Search properties and other platforms owned by Alphabet, so it will track with the price of the clicks and also the mix of clicks being counted. Grey Matter’s estimate instead tracks the same keywords across 14 advertisers.

    There is no direct confirmation or contradiction between the two figures since they measure entirely different things.

    According to recent reports, grey Matter’s report holds the keyword and the account constant, while raw CPC averages also rise when advertisers buy different clicks. With 14 clients of one agency and a range from 1% to 44%, the report is a reference point for B2B non-brand Search, not a forecast for any single account.

    According to recent reports, you can run a same-keyword check on your own account by comparing the year-over-year change in what the same non-brand keywords cost with the change in the account’s average CPC. The report reads the gap between those two as the effect of keyword, match type and bid strategy changes. A same-keyword rise can still include the effect of higher spending.

    Grey Matter’s data runs through September, so it doesn’t include fourth-quarter auctions. For 2027 budgets, the report’s guidance is to scale them gradually and assess each step by how much the additional clicks cost. For campaigns on automated bidding such as Maximize Conversions, the report also suggests deciding what the additional conversions are worth before raising the budget, and setting a target to match.

    Student journalists are reporting more local news for real audiences. Their professors are exhausted.

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3523 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • Recent findings suggest that we will never sell your address.
    • We have sent a confirmation link to .
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Recent findings suggest that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    A fresh study finds that journalism school faculty — charged with putting more student work in front of non-student readers — often serve as a hidden infrastructure for local news. Burnout is a risk.

    If there’s one substantial takeaway from the past two decades of local news struggle — the often perilous, occasionally brilliant transition from dominant newspapers to online media — perhaps it’s this: Passion alone isn’t enough.

    According to recent reports, A newspaper newsroom filled with committed editors and brilliant reporters still stares into the same headwinds as its more middling peers. The devotion of those leading a nonprofit outlet can mean little if revenue can’t keep the doors open. And even when the money is less key — when journalism is somewhat protected from the demands of the market — passion is still a finite resource, and it’s not always renewable.

    Sources indicate that that truism came to mind when I was reading a recent article by Sima Bhowmik of the University of Vermont and Andrea Lorenz of Kent State. It looks at one specific corner of the contemporary news ecosystem: journalism schools that use their students to fill voids in local coverage.

    According to recent reports, J-schools, after all, have faculties full of experience and students who need it. A few decades ago, an early-career journalist might have spent a few years covering city council meetings and school board budgets before moving up the chain to a bigger outlet. That path barely exists these days, and journalism programs know their students need the chance to do real work. What if these reporters-in-training could handle some of the local stories that the city’s daily no longer can?

    It has been revealed that RELATED ARTICLEA “win-win” partnership brings a surge of reporting firepower to hyperlocal news outlets around BostonSarah ScireNovember 13, 2025RELATED ARTICLELen Downie: The teaching hospital model works, but it will require drastic changeLeonard Downie Jr.September 12, 2012If you happen to live near a college with a journalism program, you’ve probably seen this idea — often called the “teaching hospital” model — in action. Here in the Boston suburbs, many of the stories I read about my town are written by Boston University students. According to UVM’s Center for Community News, where Bhowmik is an assistant research professor, there were 282 such efforts as of 2025, producing local news inside 205 colleges and universities. Those numbers were up from 227 programs in 172 colleges the year before — a boom fueled by a surge in philanthropic funding for these partnerships.

    Bhowmik and Lorentz’s paper — published in Journalism & Mass Communication Educator — is the result of interviews with 118 faculty and staff at 101 of those colleges, and their major takeaway is one that will be familiar to many in local news: They’re exhausted.

    In a recent development, participants repeatedly used phrases such as “at capacity,” “don’t have the bandwidth,” “not enough hours of the day,” and “it’s just a lot” to describe the workload. Several described long workdays and exhaustion, with one participant saying the amount of editing “just about kills me every semester.” At many institutions, faculty workload was intensified by staffing shortages, retirements, hiring freezes, and budget cuts. This left faculty with little time to provide the one-on-one coaching necessary to elevate student stories to publishable quality… “What’s happening in the academic ecosystem is so phenomenal, thanks to these really passionate founders on the faculty,” Bhowmik told me. “But the extra work they’re putting it isn’t always getting acknowledged within the system. A professor might be editing 10 or 20 stories a week, by students without much experience, on top of a full teaching load. There’s a lot of overwork and some dissatisfaction, even though they know how key the work is.” (See above: Passion alone isn’t enough.) Here’s how one faculty member described their situation: Think about it: Like, how many reporters does the average assigning editor at a mid-sized newspaper supervise? Half a dozen? So try, like, 20 of them, and each of them is writing for a different outlet maybe, which has its own set of deadlines and editor. And they’re all at varying skill levels, and broadly, they’re all pretty upcoming. Their copy requires a lot of work, their reporting often requires a lot of handholding. Another talked about the responsibility of getting student work up to the level a news outlet expects. You can’t just give a meh student story a C- and be done with it if a local editor is expecting publishable copy. It takes a lot of work to get student work up to the quality of professionally published work. And a lot of students start out with really good ideas, do some good reporting by the time they’re done in the semester, it needs work, and that tends to fall on the faculty person. And that’s a lot of work outside of uncompensated work…But bridging that gap between what a student produces at the end of a semester and what can actually be published is still a massive gap that needs to be addressed. And aside from the editing work, faculty described the administrative burden of being the connective tissue joining two distinct worlds. Negotiating pitches, coordinating deadlines, dealing with revisions, shepherding copy flows — all of it with students who are juggling other courses, work-study jobs, and the life of college student — can be “difficult to sustain without administrative support, dedicated staff, or funding for editors,” they write. Just to save a few dozen proud Mizzou alums from emailing me: Yes, the “teaching hospital” model is not a new idea. The idea of giving journalism students real-world experience in public-facing outlets has been central to the Missouri Method for more than a century, and other major journalism schools have long done versions of this work. But Bhowmik notes that many of these new efforts are in smaller colleges with smaller journalism programs — places without the in-house infrastructure of a Columbia Missourian or KOMU, where media partnerships involve more ongoing negotiation. That can leave more of the pressure of sustainability on one or two overworked faculty members. As Bhowmik and Lorenz put it: …faculty labor is not incidental to the model; it is the hidden infrastructure that allows student work to move from classroom assignment to public-facing journalism. We argue that passion may help launch these programs, but passion alone is not a sustainable staffing model. If universities treat these initiatives as ordinary courses while expecting faculty to function simultaneously as instructors, editors, partnership managers, and newsroom supervisors, the model remains vulnerable to burnout and institutional instability. None of this, of course, is to say that these academic-publisher partnerships aren’t performing valuable roles in hundreds of communities. These programs have generated thousands of stories that otherwise might never have reached the public. But the sort of exhaustion Bhowmik and Lorenz describe reminds me a lot of what we saw in the first wave of local nonprofit news outlets in the late 2000s and early 2010s. Many of those were founded by idealistic journalists — often refugees from the local daily — who saw the opportunity to do something new and valuable for their communities. They put in long hours editing stories, selling ads, pitching foundations, and building audiences. And within a few years, a lot of them were burnt out, and their outlets suffered for it. In the decade-plus since, funders have gotten smarter about building institutional capacity — knowing that passion can only fuel so much. The world Bhowmik and Lorenz describe inside these journalism programs makes me think that department chairs and deans would be wise to consider a similar pivot to make these academic-publisher partnerships sustainable for the long term.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Clerk is on a mission to solve user management once and for all. We are a globally distributed team dedicated to providing best-in-class developer experience, with obsessive attention to every detail. Today, we provide developers with full-stack React components and hooks like , , , useUser, and useOrganization. These APIs allow developers to build hard-to-get-right user and organization management flows. We believe that a component is worth a thousand APIs.

    Our Dashboard is a primary tool for configuring our components, as well as a centralized place for managing your app’s owners.

    Industry observers note that you’ll join Visual Designers, UI Engineers, and fellow Product Designers on the Clerk Design team to build our core product, the Clerk Dashboard. You’ll always keep developer experience first as you gain a deeper understanding of the business needs of user management. You’ll optimize for customer delight, flexibility, and ease-of-use within a complicated, technical domain.

    Recent findings suggest that collaborate with teammates to design new features. You’ll work closely with Product, Design, and Engineering across project lifecycles from ideation to implementation.

    Gather requirements. You’ll research the technology and customer impetus behind the features we release. You’ll attain a deep understanding of the problems we solve.

    Recent findings suggest that structure and prototype. You’ll create flows and interactions that make sense of complex information, whether it’s a static component or a multi-page view.

    In a recent development, not settle for less than pixel-perfection. You’ll work with a world-class UI Engineering team to bring your Figma frames to life. You set the bar for quality.

    Elevate our design culture. You’ll support and expand the Clerk Design visual language, component library, accessibility practices, design system, and design processes.

    It has been revealed that you’re a Senior(+) level Product Designer with experience working in authentication, user management, or developer tools. You love your craft. You push Engineers to build experiences they’re unsure if they’re capable of (and you expect them to do the same for you).

    In a recent development, you’re in the Americas. The Clerk Design team is spread across the globe; Product Design currently spans UTC+1 to UTC+5:30. You live in a location that is ±3 hours within U.S. Mountain Time (MDT, UTC−06:00).

    Sources indicate that you have technical fluency. You have a deep understanding of designing interactive software on the web. You don’t need to author production-ready front-end code, but it’s a significant plus if you can.

    You work iteratively. Your process embodies a “ship and iterate” mentality. You value the quick pace of a growing startup like Clerk.

    According to recent reports, you own your time. You’re a self-starter who would rather find a tough problem to solve instead of waiting for a upcoming task. To be successful at Clerk, you need to make the most of the autonomy you’re given.

    According to recent reports, 💰 Competitive Salary – We want you to know that we value the skills and experience you bring to the table. We go out of our way to make sure that you feel fairly compensated.

    📈 Equity Ownership – At Clerk, we believe in shared success. That's why we offer a stock option initiative so that everyone can benefit from the growth and prosperity of the company.

    Sources indicate that ⚕️ Health Coverage – We care about your well-being. That's why we offer top-tier health insurance to ensure that your health needs are fully met.

    Sources indicate that 🎧 Work Gear - Set up your ideal home office with the gear of your choice. At Clerk, we want to ensure that you have everything you need to perform at your best.

    🏖️ Flexible Vacation Policy – We believe in work-life balance and trust you to take the time you need. Although we recommend 25 days per year, our vacation policy is unlimited. This is in addition to observing national holidays specific to your country of residence.

    Sources indicate that 🌍 Diverse and Inclusive Team – Join our exceptional, diverse, and globally distributed team at Clerk. We are committed to fostering an inclusive environment where everyone can contribute their best in building impactful products and tools for the modern web.

    Recent findings suggest that canada’s proposed federal budget includes some good news for local journalism. The federal government is extending its journalism tax credit by $501 million, expanding eligibility to audio and audiovisual news organizations, and renewing the Local Journalism Initiative, which supports journalism in underserved communities.

    RELATED ARTICLEIn Canada, a government program to support local news tries to determine who’s most deservingSarah ScireMay 8, 2020Sarah wrote about the Local Journalism Initiative in its early days. A study earlier this year found that reporters paid with LJI funding believed they maintained their roles as watchdogs and wrote balanced stories, though two-thirds of interviewees were concerned about the perception of a conflict of interest. A growing number of journalists say the benefits of government subsidies for journalism outweigh the drawbacks.

    A recent report in The Tyee suggests government support is essential to the survival of local media in Canada. (The Tyee has received support from the Local Journalism Initiative.).

    According to recent reports, “It’s either this or death, frankly,” LJI program director and Canadian Association of Journalists president Brent Jolly told The Tyee. “It’s not about local news editors getting their marching orders from the Prime Minister’s Office like some conspiracy theorists want you to think. It’s about infrastructure.”.

    Lisa Sygutek, publisher of the Crowsnest Pass Herald in Alberta, credited the LJI with growing the publication from “a 16-page paper to a 24-page paper.”.

    Read more in The Tyee’s look at Canadian local news here.

    #20443. ChatGPT Ads Vs. Google Search Ads: What Early Data Highlights via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    ChatGPT Ads Vs. Google Search Ads: What Early Data Highlights via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2437 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that this past week, OpenAI rolled out cost-target bidding in its ChatGPT Ads platform.
    • The question for a paid search team is whether ChatGPT Ads now compete with Google Search Ads for advertising dollars, and whether the early results make a case for moving some of their budget to ChatGPT Ads.
    • ChatGPT Ads are competing for advertisers’ budgets.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that this past week, OpenAI rolled out cost-target bidding in its ChatGPT Ads platform. These ads first rolled out in February. By Aug. 31, OpenAI reported that its ads product had achieved a $1 billion annualized run rate.

    The question for a paid search team is whether ChatGPT Ads now compete with Google Search Ads for advertising dollars, and whether the early results make a case for moving some of their budget to ChatGPT Ads.

    ChatGPT Ads are competing for advertisers’ budgets. However, the revenue metrics, survey data, and Google’s disclosures I reviewed give no indication of how many dollars have been diverted away from Google Search Ads to ChatGPT Ads.

    Industry observers note that in terms of performance metrics, a ChatGPT ad click visit to an advertiser’s website generated about one-third the revenue of a paid search visit in U.S. traffic. The working paper in my Nov. 2 coverage provided the pooled revenue metric from 102 different websites with transaction and revenue tracking. The authors of that paper called the comparison descriptive. One of the authors’ universities also released a press statement saying that for every dollar an advertiser spends on ChatGPT Ads, they receive $0.52 back in revenue (compared to $3.40 for every dollar spent on Google Search).

    Only the first of these performance metrics was actually measured. The second figure combined that measured performance metric with the average cost-per-click pricing from one ChatGPT account and the median cost-per-click pricing from 16 paid search accounts. So the second figure varies with what an advertiser pays per click on each of those channels.

    An Oct. 21 engineering post from OpenAI puts the run rate above $1 billion, with more than 100,000 advertisers having run ads since launch. Alphabet reported $63.35 billion in Search & other revenue for the third quarter, up 12%, which I covered on Oct. 28.

    On Alphabet’s earnings call, Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler cited “the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode” as one factor in slower Search growth, without giving a figure or a baseline.

    Google Search was the most-mentioned potential source of future ChatGPT ad spending in a Bank of America survey of 117 advertisers and agencies, TheStreet reported on Oct. 14. I haven’t seen the bank’s note, and the survey asked about plans. It doesn’t measure money that has moved.

    Neither organization’s revenue figures show spending that shifted from one platform to the other. Google can continue to grow even as some advertisers move part of their budgets elsewhere.

    According to recent reports, in U.S. traffic, paid search generated $2.45 in revenue per session versus $0.89 with ChatGPT ad sessions, and transactions per session came to 1.17% against 0.37%.

    These pooled figures are based on a total of 60 weeks (through Aug. 22). For U.S. traffic, there were up to 28 weeks of ChatGPT ad sessions available for analysis.

    Recent findings suggest that kaiser and Schulze built a statistical model that controlled for website, device type, and week, and found that ChatGPT ad sessions generated lower rates of conversion and lower revenue per session than paid search. These results were robust even after removing individual advertisers. Out of 87 different advertisers who used both paid search and ChatGPT ads in U.S. traffic, 84 produced less revenue per session using ChatGPT ads.

    According to recent reports, about 20% of the 102 websites studied were services, software, education, or finance websites. A table footnote explains that these websites report online conversions as bookings, leads, licenses, or sign-ups. However, the appendix calls a transaction a completed order, and it does not explain how the authors defined the relationship between these two types of metrics.

    Recent findings suggest that because advertisers chose to buy ChatGPT ads, the authors do not argue causally that ChatGPT is worse for advertisers than paid search. Rather, the authors view their work as “descriptive rather than causal,” a record of what these websites received from each advertising channel. They do not provide any evidence as to whether switching advertising dollars from paid search to ChatGPT under matched campaigns would be beneficial or detrimental to specific advertisers.

    Data for this study were donated by Grips Intelligence, where Kaiser, a former employee, works as a scientific advisor. The authors disclose that Kaiser has received a salary and virtual company shares from Grips Intelligence. The authors add that Grips Intelligence played no role in conducting the research described in this study.

    I contacted OpenAI about this study and received an email response from an OpenAI spokesperson saying the study “captures an earlier period of ChatGPT Ads’ development and extrapolates platform performance from a small sample.” The statement also indicates OpenAI has kept launching products since the ads rolled out, with Target CPA and Target CPC among the recent ones.

    Kaiser and Schulze express the difference in terms of value for money, revenue per session divided by click price. Treating each session as a paid click, that works out to about $0.52 per ad dollar for ChatGPT ($0.89 ÷ $1.72) and $3.40 for search ($2.45 ÷ $0.72), the two figures in the Frankfurt School release. The authors report that an ad visit from ChatGPT returns about one-third the value of a search visit at about 2.4 times the price. In their abstract, they state that ChatGPT ads are worth less than a sixth the value for money of Google Search. A table provides a reported ChatGPT price of 6.57 times what would be necessary to produce the same return on investment as Search.

    The Frankfurt School release cites the difference as “6.6 times better value for money” for Google and reports this in revenue per ad dollar. Its $0.52 and $3.40 figures are not provided within the body of the paper, and the release itself gives no explanation of how they were calculated.

    Industry observers note that there is no single price given for search, but rather a median price of $0.72, which comes from 16 mostly U.S. accounts that have linked Google Ads cost records. This price was not matched to the revenue each site generated.

    It has been revealed that the ChatGPT price is $1.72, which Opascope, an agency that runs paid media for clients, published in June. It covers one account and about $60,000 in spend over 15 days, on campaigns the agency scaled after they demonstrated promise. Opascope wrote that the numbers aren’t an average of every test it debuted, and it reported a 1.49x ROAS.

    Just one website in the sample did as well as Opascope’s account on both conversion rate and implied revenue per visit, and it had only nine ChatGPT ad sessions.

    According to recent reports, the authors suggest that $1.72 is a conservative price as it is toward the low end of what practitioners report and below the $3-$5 OpenAI suggests be used as a starting maximum bid. Also, bidding is based on a maximum value, which is simply the cap an advertiser sets, not necessarily what each click will cost.

    In a recent development, resampling advertisers, while keeping the search price constant, gives the authors a range of $0.05 to $0.57 around a ChatGPT click price of about $0.26 that would match search’s return. Neither the ChatGPT click price nor the search price was changed.

    Advertising agencies have provided reports about their individual ChatGPT Ads campaign data for one advertiser, and separately, Brooke Osmundson reported in September that advertisers lacked the context to assess what they were being told by the numbers in such reporting.

    Sources indicate that stubGroup provides ChatGPT ads management services. It ran Google ad campaigns and ChatGPT Ads campaigns for an advertiser who is a B2B compliance manufacturer, for 30 days. The clicks on ChatGPT ads cost $0.76 a click. The clicks on Google search campaigns cost $10.46 a click. The cost per lead with ChatGPT was $92.21; with Google it was $157.57. The conversion rates were 0.8% with ChatGPT, and 6.64% with Google.

    In a recent development, the agency remarked that while the advertising campaigns run through Google have years of optimization behind them, the leads generated through those campaigns appear to be converting to customers at a greater rate so far than the leads generated through ChatGPT ads. As a result of this, the cost per customer appears to be lower for Google. How many customers will be ultimately generated from the leads created through both platforms, StubGroup does not yet know, due to the client’s long sales cycle. Additionally, the agency said that the $0.76 per click was low when compared to the CPCs of some of its other clients.

    Workshop Digital used its own funds to pay for $2,319 worth of clicks on ChatGPT Ads. Workshop Digital’s CPC for ChatGPT ads was $3.14. For Google Search the CPC was $6.76. The CTR for Workshop Digital’s ChatGPT ads was 1.1%. For Google, the CTR was 5.2%.

    Recent findings suggest that workshop Digital received zero qualified leads from its ChatGPT ads, and two qualified leads from Google. The agency called the two types of advertising campaigns “not a direct comparison,” although it didn’t provide the spend amount or dates for Google Search as part of the comparison.

    Brafton, which sells ChatGPT Ads services, ran one click campaign with one ad from June 17 to Aug. 28. It spent $1,524.11 for 263 clicks and one form submission. Its Google and LinkedIn comparisons are outside benchmarks, and its director of paid media, Zach Shah, remarked ChatGPT ads are “priced like search, but seem to behave like paid social.”.

    All three agency reports came down to what happened after the click, the stage with the fewest results.

    Additionally, OpenAI pointed me to some customer success stories via its ad page. One such example is from Jotform. According to this example, their cost per signup is approximately 30% less than with paid search. This figure is based on Jotform’s internal data collected during July; however, no costs are provided behind it, nor does it detail how the sign-ups were attributed. Sign-ups do not equal sales.

    A paid search team may be asked to shift some portion of search spend to ChatGPT on the strength of a per-dollar figure based upon another party’s click costs. For an account paying a number of dollars per click on search, a number greater than the median of the paper’s data, there are differing starting points for making such comparisons. The basis for comparison that makes sense begins with actual spend and attributed revenue on each channel for the same period of time and using the same attribution settings.

    Sources indicate that the size of the test will affect how much an ecommerce account testing ChatGPT Ads can learn from a weak result. In all, 18 of the paper’s 102 sites recorded transactions resulting from ChatGPT ads; a single zero does not distinguish a weak channel from a small test. So when reporting to stakeholders, the number of sessions associated with each ad campaign belongs beside the revenue figures, because what a zero means is quite different depending on whether there were a few dozen or a few thousand visits.

    In a recent development, to compare results, lead-gen accounts also need to define a qualified lead in exactly the same terms on both channels and give those leads sufficient opportunity to convert. This is why StubGroup’s customer comparison is still open, since its lower-cost leads have not yet turned into lower-cost customers. While a cost per signup was used by Jotform as the metric in their case study, it is further removed from revenue than a cost per customer.

    A team planning to present Ads Manager results either against the paper’s data or against its Google Ads performance metrics will first need to document its attribution settings. On OpenAI’s Measure Results page, Ads Manager conversion totals may include eligible view-through conversions, and advertisers select from a 7-day, 14-day, or 30-day click window. The view-through window can be set to one day or disabled, and both windows employ last-touch logic. The paper tracked visits that were attributable to the ad.

    According to recent reports, ads Manager tracks clicks, while analytics uses sessions. There can be differences between these two numbers. On OpenAI’s basics page, the firm states ad-review crawling programs may access landing pages that contain tracking parameters, and analytics tools may report these visits as paid traffic even if they do not represent billable clicks. The Measure Results page provides additional explanations for these discrepancies, including redirects, consent settings, and browser-based blocking. Only by assuming clicks and sessions align can the release’s $0.52 be calculated from reported revenue per session and cost per click.

    OpenAI’s ads FAQ claims that they do not right now provide performance benchmarks. In addition, all four OpenAI help pages I reviewed provided a suggested starting bid, but none provided any information about click prices across advertisers. Neither did OpenAI’s statement. One advertiser’s cost is documented in the research paper. Each agency CPC was unique to its specific case.

    There were no monthly or bid-type breakdowns within the research paper, so it could not establish if the outcomes had been affected by OpenAI adding conversion-optimized campaigns in June. Data from the research paper ceased prior to when OpenAI implemented bid adjustments, which went into effect this month.

    Sources indicate that on Oct. 28, Google published an ads post stating that CTR for sponsored and organic product listings in AI Mode were similar. This was based on two weeks of internal U.S. data. Google gave no absolute rates. That was the single performance figure for AI Mode ads in my review of Google documentation.

    Industry observers note that two of the bid options now offered for latest ChatGPT Ads campaigns didn’t exist during the paper’s data window. Since Nov. 9, new conversion campaigns that want a cost target use Target CPA, and new click campaigns can use Target CPC, as I covered this week. The option with no cost target is Intelligent bidding, previously named Maximize Results, according to OpenAI’s bidding page. Beginning with Nov. 18, all values submitted using the legacy API bid fields are treated as the average-cost target when creating a new campaign or changing an ad group’s bid type. Max Bid and Max CPC will officially retire for existing campaigns on Jan. 1, 2027.

    It has been revealed that performance improvement is not shown in the new options. Noting which objective, bid strategy, and attribution windows produced each fourth-quarter result will help a team decide if the metrics generated this year have enough similarities to compare next year.

    #20439. AI is becoming an information gateway. Audiences still don’t want it making their news.

    📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1693 w)

    AI is becoming an information gateway. Audiences still don’t want it making their news.

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1693 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • We have sent a confirmation link to .
    • An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries noted they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries noted they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

    In my Nieman Lab prediction this time last year, I wrote that “in 2026, the use of AI as an information gateway will only rise further.”.

    As it turns out, I was right. In fresh research that I published with my colleagues Rasmus Kleis Nielsen and Richard Fletcher, one of our many findings is that generative AI systems are becoming ever more significant information intermediaries, both when intentionally used and when incidentally encountered.

    For our new report, “Generative AI and News Report 2026: From Standalone Tools to Information Infrastructure,”  we surveyed audiences across nine countries, including the United States, on their use of AI in their everyday lives, what they think its impact will be on different sectors of society, and what they think about its use in news and journalism specifically. I obviously think you should read the whole report, but here are some of the major takeaways.

    Industry observers note that the use of standalone conversational AI systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini continues to grow rapidly, with 51% of respondents across the six countries where we have past data saying they now use AI weekly (49% in the U.S.). That’s a faster spread, at least in the U.S., than smartphones or the internet saw.

    Many people also encounter AI through “incidental” AI exposure in the AI-infused services and platforms they’re already using. Search engines such as Google and Bing are key drivers: 57% of respondents across countries mentioned they saw or engaged with AI-generated answers or summaries in the last week. News media, too, drives AI exposure. An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

    Despite all the talk about AI agents, we find that, so far, they haven’t broken into the mainstream. The vast majority of respondents across all nine countries (67%) noted they had not used an AI agent in the last week. Fourteen percent used one for a real task and 13% tried one just to experiment.

    Recent findings suggest that our data provides solid evidence that a broader transformation of the information environment is afoot. Conversational AI systems have arrived as information intermediaries. Trust is not the main reason people use them. Instead, people see conversational AI systems as friction-reducing machines that get them information more rapidly.

    In a recent development, “Getting information” continues to be the most common use case. Thirty-eight percent of respondents across countries (35% in the U.S.) said they had used generative AI for getting information in the last week, up from 24% in 2025 and 11% in 2024.

    We looked more closely at what people do when they say they use AI for getting information. Across the six countries we’ve surveyed since 2024, we primarily see a mixture of search-equivalent behaviors like “researching a topic” (24%) or “answering factual questions” (18%). People are also increasingly turning to AI for advice (20%).

    Recent findings suggest that using AI directly for news, meanwhile, remains a niche activity, as we demonstrated in the Digital News Report earlier this year. But that use is increasing: 9% of respondents across our six core countries say they use AI for news, up from 6% in 2025 and 3% in 2024.

    Recent findings suggest that many people don’t hold clear or strong views about whether AI output is trustworthy. But people who do rely on it for information trust it. Across the nine countries, 75% of those who used AI to answer factual questions trusted the answers, as did 76% of those who used it for advice and 72% of those who used it for news. Only small minorities expressed distrust.

    It has been revealed that at the same time, trust and trustworthiness do not, at this stage, seem to be central to why people rely on AI systems. Instead, people tend to see these systems as friction-reducing machines. The convenience of getting a faster and easier answer was chosen by 64% as the main reason they use AI, followed by the interactivity afforded by natural language interfaces (56%). Only a minority (21%) stated they use AI because they get more reliable information from it than from other sources.

    As AI systems become widely used, their growing popularity is likely to affect the use of legacy content offerings and digital platforms and services. As my coauthor Rasmus Kleis Nielsen put it on LinkedIn, rapid growth in AI use isn’t just eating into what news sites have to offer. It’s eating into search, too — with people who use AI for information saying they use not just news, but search engines less, too, and by a wider margin. Challenging times may be ahead not just for news publishers, but also for the incumbent digital giants previously seen as unassailable.

    As in previous years, we wanted to know what people think of AI’s use in journalism and news. We find that people’s attitudes here are remarkably entrenched and negative — though they also haven’t worsened significantly.

    Recent findings suggest that people across countries remain uncomfortable with the use of AI in the newsroom, especially with the idea of news being made entirely or primarily with AI. On average across nine countries, just 12% of respondents say they are very or somewhat comfortable with news made entirely by AI. That figure rises to 19% if there is some human oversight. This has hardly changed since 2024, and the gap between human- and AI-made news appears in every country we surveyed.

    This also remains true regardless of whether it is breaking news or reporting. People are even more uncomfortable with AI being used for commentary or opinion — formats where the expectation that a human should share their view is strongest.

    Our findings raise several important questions for journalists and publishers navigating the rise of generative AI.

    First, generative AI is becoming an increasingly significant information intermediaries, with a number of possible knock-on effects on news. People are using AI to reduce friction by getting “good enough” outputs for some information needs — and skipping legacy platforms, established publishers, and the time and effort it takes to find the best available information. Discovery, brand attribution, data collection, and monetization all grow more challenging for publishers in this context.

    In a recent development, second, even though use continues to grow, the public remains skeptical of AI in news. This isn’t just a challenge for newsrooms’ internal adoption. It also highlights that publishers using AI need to communicate to audiences what’s in it for them.

    According to recent reports, third, beyond news, our findings speak to wider debates about AI’s societal impact. As in other studies on this topic, we find that uptake of AI is uneven. Weekly use is more common among people in professional occupations than those in entry-level or service occupations. Most people rely on free — usually less advanced — AI models.

    Sources indicate that the differences in how — not just whether — people use AI may become a new dividing line. As AI researcher and OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy recently argued, there is a widening “gap in shared understanding of LLM capability,” with most people not seeing what has left those inside AI firms both excited and worried.

    Recent findings suggest that expectations of what AI will do differ far more between daily people and people who have never used it than between any other groups in our survey. When two groups form very different views of the same technology because they have such different starting points, there will likely be consequences.

    This doesn’t matter just for people’s individual choices around whether and how to make use of AI in their own lives. It also matters where AI is adopted and governed through collective decisions — in public services, for example — that apply to those who do not use it.

    Felix Simon is the research fellow in AI, information, and news at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism and a research associate at the Oxford Internet Institute (OII) at the University of Oxford.

    When the Covid-19 pandemic normalized remote work, a second trend caught on: shutting down physical newsrooms.

    Industry observers note that A report from Northwestern University’s Local News Initiative, published Tuesday, looks at the cultural losses that news outlets face when their staff stops working together under one roof. Here’s LNI contributor and Columbia College Chicago journalism professor Jackie Spinner:.

    As pandemic-era safeguards that necessitated working from home waned, some have championed the technological advances that allow many journalists to report, edit and publish from basically anywhere with stable Internet access. But the cost savings from a smaller or nonexistent physical presence isn’t the only consideration. Less clear-cut is the impact on the elements of journalism that never appear on budgets, such as the training absorbed from looking over someone’s shoulder or the institutional knowledge gained and passed by working in proximity to others over time.

    During the pandemic, several news outlets downsized their offices — from city high-rises to co-working spaces — due to financial constraints and upcoming hybrid work schedules.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Niemanlab ↗ Open Full Page

    “A government that ‘gets it’”: Canada recommits to federal funding for news

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • We have sent a confirmation link to .
    • In a recent development, the newly introduced budget would make a local reporting program permanent and extend a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    In a recent development, the newly introduced budget would make a local reporting program permanent and extend a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries. The support makes “a massive, massive difference.”.

    Sources indicate that A Canadian program to place local reporters in underserved communities has lived from renewal to renewal. Publishers who relied on the Local Journalism Initiative couldn’t be sure whether the money would be there again.

    That changed last week when Canada proposed a federal budget that would make the Local Journalism Initiative permanent. The 2026 budget would increase LJI funding to $134 million over four years with $41 million in annual ongoing funding after that. (Figures are, naturally, in Canadian dollars.) For the budget to be finalized, it must pass Parliament. With Prime Minister Mark Carney’s party in the majority, it’s expected to.

    Expanding the LJI is not even the biggest piece of federal help for newsrooms, according to Paul Deegan, president and CEO of the news industry advocacy group News Media Canada. The same budget extends a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries through 2028 and opens it to radio and television newsrooms for the first time. The tax credit will cost $501 million over the next five years, according to the budget. Thanks to the Online News Act, Canadian newsrooms also get funding from Google. And then there’s Canadian investment in public media; the 2026 budget added $300 million over two years to CBC/Radio-Canada “to strengthen its capacity to meet the evolving needs of Canadians across the country.”.

    I asked Deegan: How did Canadian publishers secure so much federal funding for news?

    “We have a government that ‘gets it,’” Deegan remarked. “They see what Massive Tech monopolists have done to local news. They know the labor tax credit is the leading driver of maintaining and growing newsroom headcount.”.

    RELATED ARTICLECalifornia’s big local news bill becomes lawLaura Hazard OwenOctober 1, 2026There have been similar proposals and experiments in the United States, including a new tax credit in California. But Canada is much further down the road. The country can offer lessons on what it looks like when a federal government commits to supporting journalism.

    In a recent development, the labor tax credit refunds 35% of a newsroom employee’s salary, up to $29,750 per journalist per year. The percentage had been scheduled to fall to 25% at the end of 2026.

    “In terms of employing the [largest] number of journalists and keeping newsroom employment stability, the labor tax credit is number one,” Deegan said.

    There’s also the Online News Act which has brought in $100 million of Google money annually. Of that amount, $63 million is set aside for news publishers. (Meta blocked news on Facebook and Instagram in Canada rather than pay under the Online News Act.) Publishers receive around $17,000 per journalist per year.

    In a recent development, “That’s about $47,000 per journalist per year from those two measures,” Deegan stated. “That just makes a massive, massive difference.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in the U.S., some ideas for funding local journalism have been criticized as helping large chain newspapers — including chains that have hollowed out local newsrooms for years. Deegan — whose news industry group counts Postmedia and Torstar as members — acknowledged that the largest share of tax credit dollars goes to the largest employers.

    Industry observers note that but News Media Canada also represents small and digital-only publications, and Deegan noted the smallest Canadian outlets face another problem. To qualify for the tax credit, an organization must produce original news content and regularly employ at least two journalists “at arm’s length” from its owners. An advisory board found the second rule excludes small “mom-and-pop” newsrooms.

    It has been revealed that the Local Journalism Initiative is a more targeted program than the tax credit. Rolled out in 2019, it was designed to support local and community news in underserved areas. The LJI program supports about 470 reporting positions in roughly 1,000 communities across Canada.

    Recent findings suggest that even generous government subsidies have not stopped losses in local news completely. But early results highlighted the LJI increased reporting capacity and local news in “news poverty” communities with limited local news offerings. The same evaluation identified reaching “news deserts” — communities with no existing local news outlets — and Indigenous communities as obstacles.

    Sources indicate that “Since LJI is demand driven, funding allocation across the country varies and gaps remain in some areas, such as news deserts,” the report reads. Later, the report notes that allowing news startups “could better support attraction and retainment of journalists” in the neediest communities.

    Many of the newsrooms receiving the LJI funding are small. Deegan described family-owned weekly newspapers with circulations as low as 800. Funding provides a local journalist to report on “cops, courts, city hall, and the school board.”.

    “Without those LJI journalists in some of those communities, those things simply wouldn’t be covered,” he mentioned.

    In a recent development, some underserved communities, particularly in northern Canada, struggle to hire reporters given high living costs and remote locations. “Even with the grant, it’s just hard to recruit and find people,” Deegan noted.

    In a recent development, deegan points to two factors that have made Canada’s federal funding for news work. The first is distance. Publishers get LJI money from one of three administrator organizations: News Media Canada, Community Radio Fund of Canada, or the Consortium of Official Language Minority Community Media. These organizations — not the government itself — administer the funds and an independent board advises on who qualifies for the tax credit.

    “To avoid perceptions of conflict of interest, the government ensured that third parties adjudicate who receives local journalism initiative reporters and who is eligible for the labor tax credit,” Deegan said.

    The second factor applies to the Online News Act and, more generally, to Canadian politics.

    It has been revealed that “When it comes to holding those platforms to account, one of the reasons we have been successful is that we have a ban [on] corporate political financing at the federal level in Canada,” Deegan remarked. “These companies sprinkle goodies around to friendly academics, think tanks, and other useful idiots to do some of their bidding, but our government sees through that nonsense.”.

    • According to recent reports, for SEOs, this is more than an abstract concern about application security.
    • In a recent development, there have now been several recent WordPress incidents in which the trusted delivery mechanism was part of the problem, so let’s look at them together.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that I’ve worked with WordPress for more than 20 years, and for most of that time, keeping plugins updated has been among the first recommendations I’ve made when discussing website security. It’s still good advice. Known vulnerabilities don’t become less dangerous because updating a site is inconvenient. The advice does carry an assumption that most of us rarely bother to examine: The patch we’re installing is the software its developer actually intended to release.

    According to recent reports, for SEOs, this is more than an abstract concern about application security. When someone gets unauthorized access to a website, they may change the pages search engines see, introduce spam, tamper with redirects or indexing directives, or alter content without the editorial team’s knowledge. We can spend days investigating those symptoms as routine technical SEO problems while completely missing the reason they’re happening.

    In a recent development, there have now been several recent WordPress incidents in which the trusted delivery mechanism was part of the problem, so let’s look at them together. Examining them as a group is more illuminating than treating any single developer’s bad week as the big story.

    According to recent reports, in June 2024, malicious updates appeared in several WordPress.org-hosted plugins, including Social Warfare. Wordfence’s investigation traced the compromise to developer accounts that used previously exposed credentials. The injected code could create administrator accounts and exfiltrate information, and researchers also found code designed to inject SEO spam. Roughly 35,000 installations were potentially exposed, although Wordfence couldn’t say how many had actually received the malicious updates. This is an especially useful example for our profession because the search-related damage wasn’t hypothetical: SEO spam was part of the attacker’s toolkit.

    According to recent reports, the following July, Gravity Forms disclosed that some copies of versions 2.9.11.1 and 2.9.12 available for manual download had been modified maliciously. According to Gravity Forms’ incident notice, the exposure was confined to particular manual downloads and Composer installations during July 9-10, 2025. Its separate automatic-enhancement service was not compromised. That distinction is key. Two organizations could have been using ostensibly the same software while facing different risks because they obtained it through different channels.

    The more recent incident involved Rank Math SEO PRO. Rank Math’s incident disclosure indicates a subset of version 3.0.123 packages downloaded or updated from October 15 at 20:02 UTC through October 16 at 07:12 UTC contained malware capable of compromising sites if activated. Rank Math removed the affected files, provided a clean 3.0.124 release, and advised affected customers to treat their installations as compromised. Wordfence’s advisory classified the glitch as critical, with a CVSS score of 9.8. The free Rank Math plugin distributed through WordPress.org was not affected.

    It has been revealed that the three cases aren’t identical. One involved compromised developer accounts and poisoned repository updates, another concerned certain official manual downloads, and the third affected specific packages of a commercial SEO plugin. They do, however, share a problem that ordinary patch advice doesn’t adequately address: the site owner could get into trouble while obtaining software from a source they had good reason to trust.

    It has been revealed that the Rank Math release timeline makes this unusually clear. According to the Rank Math changelog, version 3.0.123 appeared on Oct. 7, but the affected distribution window didn’t begin until Oct. 15. A site reporting that version number might have received the original clean files or a compromised package, depending on when it was updated. The installed version alone cannot resolve the question.

    Industry observers note that imagine managing a hundred client sites, or an enterprise portfolio with different brands, teams, and hosting providers. A security advisory comes out and somebody asks which properties are exposed. You can generate a tidy plugin inventory in minutes, but a spreadsheet of version numbers may not tell you what was actually installed. You need deployment timestamps, a record of the package source and, where possible, a way to compare the installed files with verified clean artifacts. Gravity Forms presented a related challenge because the installation method determined whether a particular download was implicated.

    I don’t expect SEO practitioners to start auditing build pipelines. I do expect us to understand the limits of the information we routinely use to assess the health of a site. A dashboard that claims a plugin is current doesn’t certify that the underlying files are trustworthy, and installing a clean update doesn’t necessarily remove accounts, backdoors, or stolen credentials left behind during a compromise.

    See also: From Plugins To Performance: What CMOs Need To Ask About Their WordPress Stack.

    It has been revealed that in an enterprise environment, ownership of the website is often split across several groups. Marketing may choose the SEO software, development handles deployments, a hosting provider manages updates, and security gets called when someone notices suspicious activity. The SEO team is nevertheless expected to account for what the search engines can crawl, index, and understand. Those responsibilities overlap whether the organizational chart acknowledges it or not.

    Consider how a compromise might first appear in our regular work. Search Console begins reporting unfamiliar URLs. A crawl finds redirects that weren’t present last week. Canonical tags have changed without a corresponding release, or the rendered page no longer matches what the content team published. Depending on the attacker’s access, visitors, and crawlers might even be served different content. None of those observations proves a security breach, and I am not suggesting they were documented outcomes of the Rank Math incident. They are reasons to include compromise in the set of explanations we consider instead of assuming every unexpected technical change is a configuration error.

    Recent findings suggest that that can be particularly consequential when an SEO has spotted a symptom but doesn’t know whom to tell. We don’t need to become the malware response team. We do need an established route for escalating suspicious changes, preferably one worked out before an incident has everyone comparing logs and asking who owns what. The 2024 SEO-spam injection case demonstrates why that coordination belongs in an SEO conversation rather than being filed away as somebody else’s security problem.

    In a recent development, see also: Who Owns Web Performance? Building A Framework For Digital Accountability.

    WordPress itself has been looking at the trust problem. In June 2026, Matt Mullenweg announced Protect the Shire, initially describing a cooldown for upcoming plugin and theme releases before they reached sites through WordPress.org’s automatic-revision infrastructure. WordPress has also documented an automated security review process intended to identify potentially risky changes. The appeal is straightforward: a period of scrutiny may catch a compromised release before it is distributed widely, although delaying a genuine emergency fix creates a competing risk.

    In a recent development, that protection has boundaries. Commercial plugins delivered by their vendors’ own update systems don’t necessarily pass through the same WordPress.org review process, even though all the plugins appear in the same administrative interface. The FAIR project, operating under Linux Foundation governance, is taking a different approach by developing federated and independent software repositories. Protect the Shire focuses on checks within one major distribution route, while FAIR focuses on diversifying and verifying the routes themselves. Neither approach should be mistaken for a guarantee that every package reaching a website is safe.

    For people responsible for websites, the practical question is less about choosing a philosophical side in the distribution debate and more about knowing where each enhancement originates and what checks apply along the way.

    An SEO team doesn’t need to turn every plugin upgrade into a full security review. It would be useful, though, to know whether the organization retains patch dates and deployment records, whether its commercial plugins use separate delivery systems, and who can verify file integrity when a vendor identifies an affected download window. It is equally worth knowing whether the recovery plan extends beyond restoring yesterday’s backup to checking for unauthorized accounts, persistence mechanisms, and exposed credentials.

    Sources indicate that I would also ask who receives reports of suspicious URLs, unexpected redirects, or changes to indexing instructions. We already know how to inspect rendered pages, compare crawls, review logs, and investigate search performance anomalies. Those skills make us quite capable of noticing that a website isn’t behaving as it should. They don’t automatically tell us why, which is where an agreed escalation process becomes useful.

    Recent findings suggest that none of this is a reason to stop updating plugins, or an excuse to infer that a particular vendor is incompetent because it experienced an incident. The root cause of a compromise cannot responsibly be guessed from the fact that malware turned up in a package. What these examples do show is that familiar update channels and reassuring version numbers aren’t the whole story. We spend a great deal of time checking what a website actually serves rather than trusting what a configuration screen states it should serve. It seems reasonable to apply some of that same curiosity to the software we’re installing on it.

    ONA, OpenNews, and others see troubled times ahead, so it’s goodbye to “rubber chicken dinners.”.

    Recent findings suggest that RELATED ARTICLEWe know coronavirus has wrecked the events business for media in 2020. But will it come back post-virus?Joshua BentonMarch 25, 2020When the pandemic forced conferences to go virtual, the question was whether people would come back in person post-Covid.

    For a while, they did. For a couple years after the pandemic, people were excited to be in person together again. U.S. journalism organizations saw their revenue climb, as sponsors and funders spent generously.

    Recent findings suggest that at the end of 2026, though, the situation is less rosy. Combine surging jet fuel prices, inflation, media companies cutting costs, and declining sponsor and funder dollars, and the future appears grim not just for journalism conferences but, in some cases, for the organizations behind them.

    Revenue is the total revenue line on each organization’s IRS Form 990. The 990s are from ProPublica’s Nonprofit Explorer. ONA’s 990 for 2025 was not available as of November 12, 2026.

    The Online News Association noted on Tuesday that it is “pausing” its 26-year-old conference and laying off its five staffers.

    “Before the pandemic, the annual conference was ONA’s biggest source of revenue, and together with grants, it sustained the organization. This is no longer true,” Niketa Patel wrote. “The costs of large convenings have climbed sharply while professional development and sponsorship budgets have shrunk.”.

    According to recent reports, LION Publishers mentioned in September that it’s getting out of the large conference business for now. “Philanthropy is famously fickle, and funding priorities have shifted, making this kind of conference a very tough lift,” executive director Chris Krewson added.

    Industry observers note that LION barely broke even on the conferences it held in 2025 and 2026, Krewson told me. The organization may still hold smaller events next year, it’s not cutting staff or programming, and it’s expanding its Audit program. But it “won’t be taking on the responsibility for an independent event at a hotel with a food and beverage minimum and hotel room block for 400-plus people.”.

    “Every dollar I spend on rubber chicken dinners and microphones/WiFi for three days is money I can’t spend on programs that make publishers’ businesses stronger,” Krewson stated.

    OpenNews said in October that it’s switching into “emergency mode”1 and cutting back on “work that distills journalism craft: no more community calls or Source articles for at least the rest of 2026 and maybe longer.”.

    The future of OpenNews’s annual conference, SRCCON, is uncertain. “We usually make our decision about SRCCON at about this time every year, but this year is different as we consider the news from both LION and ONA and the funding pressures that we know all too well,” Jessica Morrison, co–executive director of OpenNews, told me in an email. “We are opening a community conversation today — emails going out very soon — to gather input about SRCCON, our other programs, and where we go next with OpenNews.”.

    In a recent development, the three-year-old Organization for Accessible Journalism noted Thursday that it is shutting down. “Financial support never reached a level that allowed us to build beyond an all volunteer effort — including my full-time effort,” founder Stacy Kess wrote.

    Industry observers note that journalism conferences in the United States are certainly not gone. IRE and NICAR will hold their annual data journalism conference in Denver in March. The Institute for Nonprofit News is “talking about what INN Days will look like in 2027” and will know more by early next year. And the International Symposium on Journalism is on for 2027 — its 28th year, founder (and Nieman Foundation board member) Rosental Alves told me. But things have gotten harder, he said. “It’s not only the difficulty of finding sponsors, but also the rising costs of venues, hotels, airfares, etc., compounded by shrinking travel budgets in newsrooms and even the problems international attendees face in coming to the U.S.,” he told me in an email. ISOJ cut costs, in part by moving to a different venue, and it benefits from being relatively small. “It’s very sad that foundations and corporations that funded journalism conferences in the past have pulled back their support,” Alves added. “The need for these gatherings is as great as ever.” a play on Emergency Mode for News, its initiative to support journalists working during disasters [↩].

    Take over Hub's fleet propagation mechanism from the team building its first version, and make it work for access, secrets, tenants, licences and custom roles.

    Write short design documents for foundational changes, get them reviewed by the teams that depend on them, and turn them into tested, shipped code.

    Design how Hub behaves when things go wrong: offline clusters, partial failures, Hub outages, and clusters being adopted or detached.

    Join the pod's rotations and Hub on-call, and help other builders take on backend work through reviews, guidelines and contract tests.

    Care for how a system behaves when parts of it fail, not only for the happy path.

Tech platforms would have to pay even when they surface news link previews or story snippets in their products, including AI search products. The law would also force platforms to compensate publishers when their journalism is used to train AI models.

    Any compensation would be paid through a state-run management organization, which would then distribute the funds to publishers. Platforms that don’t comply could face sanctions, including the loss of their local business permits.

    Social media and search engine companies have come out in force against the bill, with Google leading the campaign.

    Indonesia is a massive market for global digital platforms with roughly 230 million internet users. In 2023, Indonesia had the fifth-most Google users of any country in the world, with traffic reaching 4.42 billion searches.

    On Wednesday, a Google official argued that the bill would limit access to news, according to Reuters.

    Berni Moestafa, Meta’s head of public policy in Indonesia, testified that if the bill is passed “publishers could lose readership traffic as well as potential advertising and subscription revenue.”.

    Back in 2023, Canada passed the Online News Act, its own, albeit narrower law which required platforms like Google and Meta to pay publishers for sharing or linking to their content. Meta responded by blocking news links on Facebook and Instagram in Canada altogether.
